chapters.content:
## Chapter 11: The Records Room

The door to the archival station was three floors above the old pumpworks, though the water made the building’s floors uncertain. Tomas found the stairwell by following a line of blue tiles that vanished beneath the brown tide. Mara tested each step with the butt of her lamp before putting weight on it.

“Your caution is touching,” Tomas said.

“It is cheaper than replacing a leg.”

Behind them, Oris coughed into a folded sleeve. Ilya kept one hand at his elbow and the other on her medical satchel. Juno brought up the rear with her rifle held high, the cable from Mara’s restraint clipped to her belt. The guards moved in pairs, boots whispering against the damp stone.

At the landing, Mara stopped.

The air smelled of wet paper, rust, and the sweet chemical rot that had followed them through the lower district. Above the stairs stood a green iron door marked ARCHIVE—PUMPWORKS AND CIVIC FLOOD CONTROL. Someone had painted a red stripe across it. The stripe was old. The lock was new.

Tomas raised his pistol.

Mara caught his wrist. “If you shoot the lock, the room may be pressurized.”

“Rooms with paper are rarely pressurized.”

“Rooms with Council engineers are rarely sensible.”

She knelt, opened her canvas instrument case, and took out a length of signal wire. The wire had been intended for the engine. She threaded it through the lock’s inspection slit, felt for the catch, and counted the resistance beneath her fingers. One. Two. Three. On four, the mechanism clicked.

Juno looked at her. “You could have told us you knew how.”

“You could have asked.”

“That is not how command works.”

“No,” Mara said. “It is how permission works.”

The door opened on a darkness packed with shelves. Tomas entered first, then Juno. Mara followed, lamp raised.

The room had been built above the pumps on a reinforced platform. Its ceiling arched like the inside of a ship. Cabinets lined the walls, their labels painted in the old civic hand: SEAWALL MAINTENANCE, EMERGENCY ROUTING, TIDE PROJECTIONS, PERSONNEL. Water dripped from the beams but did not yet reach the shelving. Someone had prepared the station to survive the flood. Someone had known what level the water would reach.

“Don’t touch anything,” Tomas ordered.

Mara laughed once. “You brought me to an archive and object to contact.”

“I object to your conclusions arriving before the evidence.”

“Your conclusions arrived twelve years ago.”

The lamp trembled slightly in her hand. She steadied it against her ribs. Control the breath. Four in, hold two, six out. The room settled around the count.

Oris found the station’s central table beneath a tarp. Its surface held a brass index wheel and a ledger swollen nearly twice its size. Ilya scraped mold from the cover with a knife.

“Here,” she said. “Current allocations. Last three flood seasons.”

Tomas moved toward her, but Mara was already there. The first pages listed districts, pump capacities, and projected losses. The lower neighborhoods appeared in a column headed ACCEPTABLE INUNDATION. The elevated wards had no such column. Their entries were written in black ink, while the tide districts were marked in red.

“Acceptable,” Ilya said. “They wrote it down.”

“Not necessarily what it means,” Tomas replied.

Mara turned a page. “Then why is the same notation in the seawall schedules?”

She spread the ledger open. A map had been pasted into the binding, showing the old seawalls as a web of black lines. Beside each gate were instructions: reinforce North Crown, preserve Hill District, reduce pressure at South Reach. The date was twelve years old—the week before the Night of Bells.

Tomas stared at the map.

Mara felt the old room inside her open: the Signal Office, its windows bright with rain, Tomas leaning over a chart while she traced a current with her finger. They had believed the altered maps were an anomaly. They had been wrong. The choices were not hidden in one document. They had been repeated until repetition became policy.

Juno took the page from Mara. “This says they meant to let South Reach flood.”

“It says they calculated the risk,” Tomas said.

“And then accepted it.”

“Those are not the same as causing the flood.”

Mara looked at him. “You are very invested in that distinction.”

A silence passed through the room, disturbed only by the pumps groaning below.

They worked in separate corners after that. Tomas and Juno examined the routing ledgers. Ilya sorted medical evacuation manifests. Oris, sitting on an overturned crate, copied diagrams with shaking hands. Mara opened cabinet after cabinet, predicting which files had been moved, which had been hidden, which would be missing.

The current records were worse than the old ones.

Two weeks before the recent flood, the Council had ordered the closure of three relief stations in the tide districts. Their pumps were to be stripped for parts and transferred to the elevated hospital. A second order instructed crews to clear “unregistered residents” from the lower wards before the water rose. The word relocation appeared beside the labor-compound codes they had found in the buried cache.

“Here,” Tomas said.

His voice had changed. Mara turned.

He held a thin maintenance book open with both hands. Several pages bore corrections in a dark, careful script. The original entries had been scraped away and rewritten: LOCK INSPECTION COMPLETED. NO STRUCTURAL IRREGULARITY OBSERVED. CHARGE ASSEMBLY WITHIN TOLERANCE.

At the bottom of each page was a signature.

Tomas Vale.

The name seemed to possess the room. Even the pumps below quieted, as if listening.

Mara crossed to him. “You signed these.”

“I altered them.”

“After the flood.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

Tomas closed the book. “Not here.”

She seized the cover. “Here is where records are kept.”

“Here is where records burn.”

As if summoned by the word, a sharp crack sounded below. The station shuddered. Dust spilled from the ceiling. Somewhere in the pumpworks, a pressure valve screamed.

Juno shouted for the guards to check the stairs. Ilya pulled Oris upright. Mara held the maintenance book against her chest and watched Tomas calculate the room’s exits.

“Water surge,” Oris said. “The lower intake is opening.”

“Can the station hold?” Juno asked.

“For a while.”

“Define a while.”

“Longer than we have if we stay.”

Tomas pointed to the rear wall. “There’s a dry passage to the upper conduit.”

Mara did not move. “You will tell me.”

His jaw tightened. “I was under Council custody when I changed the records.”

“You were an investigator.”

“I was a suspect first. Then a witness. Then an employee, depending on which door I was standing behind.”

“You told them the lock was sound.”

“I told them the record showed it was sound.”

“You made the record.”

“Yes.”

The next tremor knocked a cabinet sideways. Files slid out like pale fish. One struck Mara’s boot. She bent and picked it up. The tab read TOWER THREE—CASUALTY ASSESSMENT. Beneath it, in red pencil: REVISE PUBLIC SUMMARY.

The pages inside listed deaths from the collapsed tower, the chemical reservoir, and the sealed shelters. A note from the Council legal office ordered the causes consolidated under one phrase: Bellmaker attack.

Mara read it twice. She had spent twelve years imagining that phrase in the mouths of strangers. Seeing it in the Council’s hand was not vindication. It was a different kind of nausea.

“You had this,” she said.

“Not this copy.”

“You had enough.”

“I had fragments. And a knife at my throat.”

She looked up. “They threatened you?”

“They threatened my sister first. Then the surviving tower keepers. Then the records themselves. They said if I testified that the lock had shifted, every evacuation order would be dismissed as the excuse of a terrorist’s accomplice.”

“You were an accomplice.”

“Yes.”

The plainness of it angered her more than denial would have. “You could have said what happened.”

“I did say what happened. I said you ignored the warning. I said you connected the reserve charge. I did not say you caused every death, because you did not.”

“You let them make me the whole disaster.”

“I let them make you the part people could hate.”

Mara stepped closer. “Coward.”

Tomas flinched, but did not look away.

“Yes,” he said. “Cowardice. And self-preservation.”

The words fell without defense around them. He explained that he had kept copies, moved them through the records office, and waited for a political opening that never came. Reform, he said, required an institution to survive long enough to change. If the Council collapsed in outrage, the city would replace it with soldiers, and the evidence would disappear beneath a clean story. So he had served the story, carefully, believing he could someday break it from inside.

Mara heard the argument and recognized its architecture. Every beam was prudence. Every locked door was necessity. It was the same structure she had lived inside: the belief that control delayed would become control regained.

“You preserved evidence by burying it,” she said.

“I preserved what I could.”

“You preserved yourself.”

“Yes.” He swallowed. “That too.”

Below them, water slammed into the pumpworks. The floor tilted. Juno ordered everyone toward the conduit. Mara tucked the casualty file into her case, then hesitated over the maintenance book.

Tomas held out his hand. “We need to carry it.”

“You mean you need to carry it.”

“I mean the dead need a record that is not only yours or mine.”

She nearly refused. Refusal was familiar; it had edges she could hold. But Ilya was watching her, and Oris was pale against the wall, and Juno was counting heads with the grim patience of someone who expected one to vanish.

Mara handed Tomas the book.

At the rear door, she stopped and looked back at the shelves. The station contained enough paper to indict a government and enough omissions to let one survive. Truth was not a bell. It did not force anyone to listen. It had to be carried, defended, interpreted—and it could be altered by the frightened hands entrusted with it.

“Move,” Juno said.

Mara entered the conduit last. Tomas followed, the records sealed beneath his coat. For once, she did not try to walk beside him or ahead of him. She listened to the water rising below and counted the others by their breathing, not to command them, but to know they were still there.

chapters.name: The Testimony
chapters.content:
## Chapter 12: The Testimony

The courtroom had no windows.

Mara remembered that first, though later she would remember the lists, the witnesses, Tomas’s hands. The room itself remained the fixed point: walls of black salt-glass, polished until the accused could see herself repeated in them. One Mara at the center table. Six Mara’s in the panels behind the judges. A thin, wavering Mara in the brass water cup. None of them looked toward the others.

The clerk read the charges beneath the city seal.

Murder by sabotage. Mass destruction. Sedition. Conspiracy to overthrow the lawful Council. Reckless endangerment of the civic floodworks. The phrases arrived in a procession, each one wearing the clean coat of a fact.

Mara counted the clerk’s breaths. Four in. Six out. Four in. Six out.

On the seventh charge, he stumbled.

She marked it as weakness.

The first witness was a mother from South Reach. Her name was Nera Pell, or perhaps Nera Pell was the name of the dead girl she carried in her testimony. Memory had made the distinction slippery. She stood with both hands locked around the rail and described the night of bells.

“There was no warning,” she said.

The prosecutor turned toward Mara. “No warning?”

“There were bells everywhere.”

“And what did those bells signify?”

“They signified that we were going to die.”

A murmur traveled through the gallery. It gathered around Mara like heat around a kiln.

The prosecutor asked whether she had seen the accused near the tower district. Whether she had heard Mara speak of making the city listen. Whether she had been told that the Bellmaker intended to punish the elevated wards.

Nera answered yes, yes, and I don’t know.

The last answer vanished from the record.

Mara heard the scratch of the court stenographer’s stylus. She watched the hand pause, then continue. In the official transcript, Nera would say that Mara had promised punishment. In the Bastion, Mara would later recite that sentence until it lost its shape.

The prosecutor did not ask about the barricades.

He did not ask why the south gates had been without power before the bells began. He did not ask why the relief boats had been reassigned, or why the northern roads had been cleared for families whose names appeared in no public evacuation notice. When Mara demanded those records, the presiding judge called them irrelevant to the question of her guilt.

“The accused is not on trial for the Council’s preparedness,” he said.

“No,” Mara replied. “Only for the part where your preparedness failed.”

Laughter rose from the gallery.

That was the moment she decided they enjoyed it.

Not the flood. She had seen too much of the flood to believe anyone could enjoy that. But they enjoyed the shape it gave them. A culprit was a wall built after the water. It did not stop anything, but it allowed everyone on the dry side to point at it and say: there. There is the reason.

The prosecutor presented casualty lists in three bound volumes. The covers were blue, the paper cream-colored, the totals printed in red. South Reach: 1,842 confirmed dead. Tide District: 3,109 presumed dead. Canal wards: 2,774 missing. The numbers made a city out of absence.

Mara recognized some names. A keeper from Tower Three. Two dockworkers who had carried the reserve charges. The boy with the copper tooth who had insisted on sleeping beside the signal batteries. Each name was placed beneath the heading BELLMAKER ATTACK.

“Do you dispute these deaths?” the prosecutor asked.

“I dispute your heading.”

“Do you dispute that you placed explosive charges in the warning network?”

“No.”

“Do you dispute that you connected the reserve charge to the central timing line?”

“No.”

“Do you dispute that Tomas Vale warned you the oldest tower’s maintenance lock was unstable?”

The courtroom seemed to contract around the name.

Mara looked at Tomas, seated behind the prosecution table. He had been given a witness’s chair but wore the gray coat of a Council investigator. His face had thinned since the night of the bells. There was a pale scar beside his mouth, one she did not remember giving him.

“I dispute the way you tell it,” Mara said.

The judge leaned forward. “The witness will answer the question.”

“Yes,” she said. “He warned me.”

A satisfaction moved through the room. It was not loud. That made it worse. Hundreds of people leaning together toward the same conclusion.

The court recessed before Tomas testified. Guards returned Mara to a holding cell beneath the chamber, where rainwater ticked through the ceiling into a drain. She stood beside it and tried to remember the clean plan: three short signals and one long, the towers seized, the hidden evacuation lists broadcast, the routes opened district by district.

But the drain made the sound of a counterweight falling.

When they called her back, Tomas was in the witness chair.

He swore to tell the truth before the same seal that had hidden the evacuation orders. His eyes found hers only once. Then they fixed on a point above her shoulder.

The prosecutor began gently.

“Were you and Mara Venn members of an unauthorized resistance?”

“Yes.”

“Did she design the attack on the warning towers?”

“She designed the first operation. The operation that preceded the bells.”

The prosecutor frowned as though correcting a child. “The operation that caused the bells.”

“Tomas,” Mara said.

The judge struck the bench. “You will not address the witness.”

The prosecutor asked whether Mara had changed the plan after he raised his concern about the lock.

“Yes.”

“Did she understand that the change could cause the tower to collapse?”

“I told her it could.”

“Did she proceed anyway?”

“Yes.”

There it was. The blade, bright and uncomplicated. Mara felt it enter, and because it was bright and uncomplicated, she believed it could explain everything.

The prosecutor brought out a diagram of the oldest tower. Tomas identified the maintenance lock, the release assembly, the counterweight. He spoke carefully, never adding a word the question did not require.

“Did Mara Venn intend to kill the citizens of Veyr?”

Tomas stopped.

The gallery stirred. Even the judge seemed to wait for the answer that would complete the monument.

“No,” Tomas said.

The prosecutor’s expression tightened. “Did she intend to cause a citywide panic?”

“She intended to force the city to hear what the Council had concealed.”

“By detonating the warning network.”

“Yes.”

“Despite your warning.”

“Yes.”

The prosecutor turned toward the judges. “And when the towers fell, when the chemical reservoir ruptured, when the gates failed—”

“I cannot say which failure caused which deaths,” Tomas interrupted.

A sharp silence followed.

Mara stared at him. He had not said she caused every death. He had not called her the architect of the flood. He had not even said that the Council was innocent. He had admitted only what she had done: the deliberate sabotage, the changed timing line, the refusal to heed his warning.

It should have been less than the truth.

Instead, it was the truth with the doors removed.

The prosecutor approached him. “Are you asking this court to excuse the accused?”

“No.”

“Are you asking it to believe the Council caused the disaster?”

“I am saying the evidence should be examined.”

“Evidence held by the accused’s organization.”

“Evidence held by the Council,” Tomas said, and his voice broke—not loudly, but enough for Mara to hear. “Including records you have refused to disclose.”

The judges conferred behind their raised screen. The prosecution objected. The objection was sustained. The records were sealed. The phrase unauthorized material entered the record in place of the evacuation scheme.

Mara watched Tomas lower his head.

He had tried to tell the truth and had still delivered her to them.

That became, in the years afterward, the center of her philosophy. Not the charge. Not the lists. Tomas.

Everyone wants a monster, she told herself. The frightened want one so their fear has a face. The powerful want one so their choices disappear behind it. The righteous want one so their righteousness can feel clean. Even the witness who knows better will feed the monster, because truth is harder to carry when it has no single throat.

The verdict came at dusk.

The court found Mara Venn guilty on every charge. The judges spoke of deliberate terror, of civic trust, of the ancient compact between the city and those who maintained its protections. They did not speak of the protected roads. They did not speak of South Reach being marked acceptable inundation. They did not speak of the lists that had named the wealthy before the bells ever rang.

The sentence was life in the Mirror Bastion, without petition for release.

Outside, citizens waited behind the barricades. Some shouted Bellmaker. Some shouted murderer. A woman spat at Mara’s boots. A boy held a paper bell cut from blue cloth.

Mara kept her breathing even as the guards chained her wrists.

Four in. Six out.

She told herself grief was another instrument of the Council. It made the dead into weights, and weights could be used to pull a person wherever power wished. Responsibility, she decided, was merely guilt dressed in a more respectable uniform.

So she carried neither.

She carried the verdict. She carried Tomas’s yes. She carried the public’s hunger for a single name.

At the Bastion gate, the mirrors multiplied her until there was no room left for the drowned.

Only one Mara remained visible: the monster everyone had agreed to need.

And behind that figure, where no court could reach, she began counting.

She has learned from the records that the Council repeatedly diverted seawalls, pumps, and rescue resources toward elevated districts and that casualty causes were consolidated under the Bellmaker narrative. She now knows Tomas altered maintenance records after the original disaster and remembers that at her trial he admitted her deliberate sabotage and refusal to heed his warning without claiming she intended every death; this testimony helped the Council condemn her while records exposing its evacuation scheme were suppressed. She carries her approved canvas instrument case with breathing gauge, tide compass, pencils, signal wire, and the recovered Tower Three casualty assessment; she remains restrained by Juno’s cable, damp, coughing, tense, angry, ashamed, and increasingly aware that her belief in society’s need for a monster has protected her from grief and responsibility.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Tomas Vale is in the upper conduit beyond the archival station with Mara, Juno, Oris, Ilya, and Council guards, directing the route toward the flood engine. He carries his route slate, concealed weapon, copied enclave records, the buried cache evidence, and the archival maintenance book showing alterations he made after the original disaster. He admitted that threats and self-preservation partly drove his concealment, while he also hoped to preserve evidence and a chance of reform. He remains guarded, damp, ashamed, and committed to carrying the records onward; Mara now also knows that at her trial he testified she deliberately sabotaged the warning network and ignored his warning, while refusing to say she intended every death or caused the entire catastrophe. Their relationship is openly confrontational but still bound by their shared history and practical dependence.

At Mara's trial, Tomas testified that she deliberately connected the reserve charge to the warning network after he warned that the oldest tower's lock could fail, but he did not claim she intended to kill citizens or caused every death; he also stated that Council records had been withheld.

The Council court convicted Mara Venn on every charge and sentenced her to life without petition for release in the Mirror Bastion, while suppressing the evacuation scheme and attributing the catastrophe publicly to the Bellmaker attack.

After the trial, Mara hardened her belief that frightened citizens, powerful officials, and even witnesses prefer a single monster because it gives fear and responsibility a manageable face, using that philosophy to avoid grief and full accountability.

chapters.name: The Engine Map
chapters.content:
## The Engine Map

Oris spread the fragments across the sloping floor of the conduit and weighted their corners with spent cartridges, a rusted hinge, and Mara’s instrument case. The pieces had come from three centuries and two disasters: a brass plate furred with green corrosion, a strip of ceramic marked in faded blue, half a surveyor’s slate, and a sheet of waterproof vellum so thin that the ink showed through on both sides.

Water whispered beneath the grating. Beyond the conduit wall, the drowned pumpworks groaned whenever the tide shifted. The sound traveled through the metal in long, patient shudders.

“Hold the lamp lower,” Oris said.

Juno moved it an inch. Oris blinked against the glare and fitted the brass plate to the ceramic strip. The edges did not meet. He turned the plate, tried again, and gave a small, irritated noise.

“That is not a map,” Ilya said. “That is a collection of things that have been stepped on.”

“It was a map before people stepped on it.” Oris coughed into his sleeve. The cough left him trembling. “And this is not a collection. It is a cross-section.”

Mara knelt beside him, the restraint cable lying slack between her wrists and Juno’s hand. She studied the lines. The old engineers had used colors that survived immersion: blue for water, red for pressure, black for access. One black line descended through the vellum, disappeared at a torn edge, then appeared on the brass plate beside a sequence of small squares.

“Gates,” she said.

Oris glanced at her. “You see that?”

“I see six diversion locks.” She touched the first square. “The original engine did not drive the tide into one channel. It balanced pressure between districts. This is the western spillway. Here is South Reach. Here—”

She stopped.

The route slate Tomas carried lay open near his knee. Its official line ran from the archival station through the upper conduit, across the old inspection bridge, and down to the engine’s outer chamber. It was a clean route, almost elegant. It avoided the lower maintenance district entirely.

Mara took the slate from him.

“You have marked the gates,” she said.

“I marked the route.”

“Which avoids them.”

Tomas’s mouth tightened. “The upper route is passable. The lower district is flooded, unstable, and sealed by Council order.”

“Sealed from whom?”

“From us, apparently.”

She laid the slate beside Oris’s fragments. The official line crossed no diversion gate. It reached the engine above the pressure works, where a technician could operate the controls without seeing what the water was being made to do. The old map showed another path: a maintenance spine running beneath the district, connecting every lock to the central chamber.

“The engine can be restarted from above,” Oris said slowly. “But not correctly. The upper controls regulate intake. They do not decide distribution.”

“And if the distribution is wrong?” Juno asked.

“The machinery will obey.”

That answer settled over them.

Mara remembered the Council cache: relocation tags, labor assignments, the authorization for priority passage. She remembered the recent pump orders transferring relief away from the lower wards. The official route was not merely safer. It was blind.

“Turn left at the inspection bridge,” she said.

Juno’s fingers closed around the restraint cable. “No.”

“The lower district is the only route to the diversion locks.”

“The route takes us outside the terms of your commutation.”

“Then the terms are worth less than the paper they were written on.”

“They were always worth less,” Ilya said. She was binding a fresh strip around Oris’s forearm, though the wound there had not reopened. “We only needed you to believe they were worth something long enough to get here.”

Mara looked at her. Ilya did not look away.

Tomas rose and took back the slate. “If we leave the marked route, the guards will report it.”

“Let them.”

“They may shoot.”

“Then stand where the bullets are not.”

Juno gave a humorless smile. “You hear her? Twelve years in a cell and she still thinks a corridor is a battlefield arranged for her convenience.”

“No,” Mara said. “I think the battlefield was arranged before we entered it.”

She lifted the vellum. Along its bottom edge, nearly erased, was a notation in the old engineering hand: *Witness all gates before resetting any.*

Oris read it over her shoulder. “That is not part of the operating sequence.”

“It is a warning.”

“It is a procedural note.”

“Those are often the same thing.”

They turned at the bridge. The guards protested first through silence: boots stopping, rifles shifting, one of them touching the signal bead at his collar. Juno made them lower their weapons, but she could not make them follow willingly. The conduit narrowed beyond the bridge, its ceiling dropping until they had to stoop. Salt glass gave way to old brick, and the dry, metallic smell of the archives became the wet stink of the maintenance district.

Mara led.

She counted junctions under her breath. Three grates. Two ladders. A pressure door with its wheel removed. At the fourth turn, the floor fell away into black water. She halted before the first guard stepped into it.

“Left wall,” she said. “There’s a service ledge.”

“How do you know?” Juno asked.

“The brick is newer.”

“That is your reason?”

“It is enough.”

The ledge carried them past a submerged stairwell. Through a broken inspection pane Mara saw a gate chamber below, its great iron doors furred with barnacles. Red paint marked a Council seal across the control housing. Someone had recently forced it open.

Juno crouched at the pane. “This district was sealed two weeks ago.”

“And yet someone is working here,” Tomas said.

A sound came from behind them. Not the tide. Boots, measured and many, striking metal in the upper conduit.

The guards looked to Juno. One raised his signal bead.

“Don’t,” she said.

He hesitated. A pulse of blue light answered from the darkness ahead: another bead, another patrol.

Juno swore and pulled Mara against the wall. “How many?”

“Eight behind,” Tomas said, peering through the pane. “At least six ahead.”

“Council patrol?” Ilya whispered.

Mara watched the blue lights advance. “They knew where we would be.”

Oris clutched the sealed engine case. “The route slate was transmitted.”

“Not the lower route,” Tomas said.

Juno reached for the nearest guard’s collar and tore away the signal bead. He flinched. She held it between two fingers, turning it until its tiny etched plate caught the lamp.

“Priority order,” she said.

“Captain?”

She read the plate. Her expression did not change, but something in her shoulders went still.

“Destroy all maintenance records in District Four,” she said. “Burn witness stores. No prisoners. If Bellmaker is encountered, return her alive.”

For a moment only the water spoke.

“One of the witnesses is us,” Ilya said.

“No,” Mara answered. “We are the reason they want the records destroyed.”

The patrol ahead shouted. Juno shoved the bead into her pocket.

“Back,” she ordered.

“There are too many,” Tomas said.

Mara looked down through the pane at the gate chamber. A lever assembly crossed the water below, connected to three manual releases. The gates had not been abandoned; they had been set in a locked intermediate position.

“Break the pane,” she said.

Juno stared at her. “That chamber is flooded.”

“So is the district.”

“Your plans improve with explanation.”

“Oris, can the lock be shifted from below?”

The engineer pressed his face to the pane. “If we can reach the housing. But the pressure—”

“Will open the west sluice.” Mara pointed. “The patrol ahead is standing over the lower spill channel.”

Tomas understood first. “You want to flood the corridor.”

“I want to move the water.”

Juno drew her rifle. “Everyone brace. And if this kills us—”

“It won’t,” Mara said.

Ilya caught her wrist before she could pull away. Her grip was surprisingly strong. “Do not say that as if certainty makes it true.”

Mara met her eyes. In Ilya’s face she saw the south shelter, the sealed doors, the family that had pounded on them while the water rose. She saw, too, the exhaustion beneath the anger.

“Then what should I say?” Mara asked.

“Say you don’t know.”

“I don’t know.”

It was a small sentence. It felt like stepping without a floor.

Juno fired into the pane. Glass burst inward. A wave punched through the opening, dragging tools and loose brick into the chamber. Oris shouted and dropped to his knees. Tomas seized the engine case while Mara looped the restraint cable around a pipe and lowered herself through the broken window.

Cold water closed over her waist, then her ribs. Below, the control housing loomed in green darkness. She found the first release by touch, its wheel jammed with mineral growth. She drove the butt of her pencil into the spokes. Once. Twice. The wheel shifted.

Above, the patrol rounded the corridor. Rifle fire cracked. Juno answered. Ilya dragged Oris behind the wall.

Mara turned the wheel until the mechanism screamed. Somewhere beyond the brick, a gate began to rise. Water tore sideways through the spill channel. The patrol ahead lost its footing; men shouted, weapons clattered, and the corridor filled with a brown surge.

“Now!” Tomas yelled.

A rope dropped. Mara caught it, but another hand closed over her forearm first. Ilya leaned through the broken pane, face white with strain.

“Take it,” Ilya said.

Mara seized the rope and climbed. Together they hauled her onto the ledge. The patrol behind them had stopped at the flooded passage. The survivors from the market tower appeared through a side hatch, Vessa in front, carrying a hooked pole and three stolen lamps.

“You took your time,” Vessa said.

Juno stared. “You followed us?”

“We followed the patrol.” Vessa pointed toward a narrow drain. “Move. They’ll close the west gate when they understand what you did.”

They fled through the drain as shots struck the brick behind them. Vessa’s people knew every turn. They passed beneath a collapsed bathhouse, through a pantry where dried fish hung above the water, and into a maintenance vault whose door was hidden behind a painted saint.

When it closed, the world became breath and dripping stone.

Ilya sat beside Mara, checking the cut along her temple. Mara held still.

“The Council is guilty,” Ilya said quietly. “They diverted the pumps. They sealed my family’s corridor. They are going to drown people again and blame you for the water.”

Mara said nothing.

“But that does not make your victims less dead.”

The words did not strike like an accusation. They landed with the blunt weight of something that had been waiting years to be set down.

“I know,” Mara said.

Ilya’s hand paused at her temple. “Do you?”

“I know the gates failed because I cut their power. I know the tower fell because I chose the charge. I know the Council was waiting for a disaster it could use.” Mara swallowed against the taste of chemicals and old smoke. “I know all of that, and still I wanted them to be afraid.”

“Wanted whom?”

“Everyone.”

Ilya wrapped the bandage and tied it firmly. “Then don’t make the engine another way to command everyone.”

Across the vault, Oris unfolded the fragments again. His hands shook, but he aligned the pieces with the route Mara had taken.

“There,” he whispered. “The lower maintenance spine reaches the central chamber. And the first diversion gate is still operable.”

Mara looked at the map. For the first time, the lines did not resemble a plan she could master. They resembled choices, each carrying water toward somebody.

“Then we witness all the gates,” she said. “Before we reset any.”

Outside, the patrol began searching the district. Inside, Vessa distributed lamps, Juno checked ammunition, and Tomas copied the stolen order into his slate.

Mara listened to the breathing of the people around her and counted none of it.

chapters.name: The People in the Shelter
chapters.content:
## Chapter 14: The People in the Shelter

The shelter had been built to withstand a flood that rose slowly.

That was what Mara remembered telling herself as she ran toward it. The south refuge stood beneath the old customs house, its doors made of ribbed iron, its walls sunk into bedrock. The engineers had designed it for twelve hundred people and stocked it for two thousand. There were cisterns, bunks, hand pumps, emergency lamps, and a control station with three independent power feeds.

A shelter, she had thought, was a promise made out of machinery.

The promise was failing.

Water rushed down the avenue behind her, carrying timber, roof tiles, a child's red shoe. The bells were still ringing. Their sound came from every direction and struck the flooded streets in waves: bronze, bronze, bronze, then the long note that seemed to pull the breath from the lungs. Mara ran with one hand pressed to the wall, counting the doors she passed.

Seven. Eight. Nine.

At the tenth door, she slipped and struck her knee. The water was already above her boots. It tasted of copper and ash. Somewhere behind the customs house, a boiler exploded with a flat, concussive thump.

She thought: the lower pumps have failed.

Then she thought: the timing line has held.

For one bright instant, the second thought overruled the first. The bells had begun as she designed them. Veyr was listening. The Council could not mute a sound that came from every tower at once. The evacuation routes would open. The hidden lists would be exposed. People would move because they had to move.

She reached the shelter plaza and saw the crowd.

They filled the steps and pressed against the iron doors, hundreds of bodies packed beneath the stone awning. Some had come from the canal wards; others wore the gray aprons of pump workers. A woman held a baby above her head. An old man was beating both fists against the left-hand door. Children screamed whenever the bells paused, because the silence made the water audible.

The gates were shut.

“Open!” someone shouted.

Mara pushed into the crowd. “Move aside. I’m with the signal works.”

A hand seized her coat. “Then open it!”

“I need the control station.”

“You need the door!”

She tore free and climbed the steps. The right-hand gate shuddered in its frame. Behind the iron, she saw faces at the narrow observation slit: wardens, shelter attendants, people already inside. One of the attendants lifted a lamp and shook his head.

The gate had no power.

Mara knew this before he mouthed the words. She could see it in the dead indicator above the locking wheel, in the slackness of the motor cable, in the way the emergency crank hung uselessly from its bracket.

“Where’s the manual release?” she demanded.

An attendant pointed toward the customs house. “Control room. Basement level. The corridor’s flooded.”

“Which corridor?”

He pointed again, this time with terror. “All of them.”

Behind Mara, the crowd surged. The door gave a low metal groan. Someone cried that the water had reached the lower street. Someone else shouted that the Council had sealed the shelter to protect the hospital on the ridge. The accusation moved through the bodies, finding mouths ready for it.

Mara believed it immediately.

The Council had done this. They had taken the power, closed the gates, and left the tide districts to drown. The shelter was proof. Every pounding fist was proof. The sealed doors made the crime visible enough to survive even the Council’s records.

She turned toward the customs house.

The entrance was a black square beneath a fallen lintel. Water poured out of it carrying papers, splintered crates, and a dead white rat. Mara pulled the signal wire from her belt and tied it around a railing so she could find the stairs again. Then she went down.

The basement smelled of fuel and wet stone.

She moved by touch. The emergency lamps had gone out, but the bells penetrated the walls, shaking dust from the ceiling. Three short notes. One long. Three short notes. One long. The pattern she had given the city had become a pulse inside the building.

At the first landing, water struck her thighs. At the second, it reached her waist. She kept one hand on the banister and counted the steps beneath her boots.

Nineteen. Twenty. Twenty-one.

A body floated past in a maintenance coat. Mara caught it by the sleeve and pulled it against the wall. The dead man’s badge read KELL, PUMP DIVISION. His eyes were open. His fingers were clenched around a ring of keys.

She took them.

The control room door stood at the end of the passage. Its inspection window glowed faintly. Mara kicked it once, twice, and the latch broke.

Inside, two Council technicians were struggling with the primary console. One had blood down his cheek. The other was trying to wrench open the cabinet beneath the gauges.

“What happened?” Mara demanded.

The older technician stared at the charges’ grease on her gloves. “You happened.”

She ignored him. “Why is the shelter line dead?”

“Because the tower network pulled every reserve feed when you overloaded it.”

“That’s impossible.”

“It’s on the board.”

He pointed. The gauges were not dark. They were crowded with needles trembling at their stops. The warning network had drawn power from the civic grid in one immense demand. The lower gates had lost their independent feed when the timing line arced through the relay house. The emergency systems were not merely switched off; they had been burned out in sequence.

Mara stepped toward the console.

“No,” she said.

The technician seized her arm. “The surge is coming down South Reach. We have to get out.”

“Restore the gate.”

“The control relay is fused.”

“Then bypass it.”

“With what power?”

She looked at the diagrams pinned behind the console. Lines ran from the tower district to the pumpworks, from the pumpworks to the shelter, from the shelter to the relief canal. Her own timing modification had turned the network into a single hungry circuit. She saw, with the cold clarity that had always been mistaken for courage, where the current had traveled.

Tower Three. Relay house. Lower pumps. Shelter gates.

The failure was not one event. It was a path.

“Open the canal diversion,” she said.

The older technician laughed once. “The diversion wheel is in the flooded chamber.”

“I can reach it.”

“You can’t stop the water.”

“I’m not trying to stop it.”

That sentence had belonged to another Mara, the one who believed every obstacle became manageable once named. She found the maintenance map and traced the route to the diversion wheel. If she opened it, the first surge would be sent toward the south canal instead of the ridge. The shelter might have minutes.

Only minutes.

She ran back upstairs.

The plaza had changed. Water covered the bottom six steps. It pushed between the crowd’s legs and dragged at loose clothing. People had begun to climb the awning supports. The baby was still held overhead, but the woman holding it was crying now, her face turned toward the iron doors.

“Where is the control station?” someone asked Mara.

She pointed to the customs house. “The diversion wheel is below.”

“Can you open the gate?”

“Yes.”

The word left her before she examined it.

She descended into the water again. The maintenance chamber lay beneath the shelter, accessible through a hatch at the back of the customs house. The key ring opened the lock on the third try. Below, the current seized her ankles and flung her against the wall.

She crawled forward.

The chamber was already filling. A great wheel stood half-submerged at its center, its spokes slick with oil. Mara reached it and wrapped both hands around the nearest spoke. She pulled. It did not move.

Above her, the crowd pounded on the gates.

The sound traveled through the stone. Not bells now. Fists. Hundreds of fists. A rhythm without pattern, a human signal no engineer had designed.

Mara braced one foot against the housing and pulled again. The wheel shifted a fraction. Somewhere beneath the floor, a gate groaned.

Then the surge arrived.

It came through the lower channel with the force of a collapsing wall. Water struck Mara’s back, tore her hands from the wheel, and drove her into the far grate. The chamber vanished in brown foam. The wheel spun once, violently, and the diversion gate slammed shut again.

Mara surfaced in darkness.

Her first thought was not for the people above. It was that the system had rejected her command.

She groped for the wheel. Her fingers found a broken spoke. She pulled herself upward, coughing, and saw a pale rectangle where the hatch stood open. Beyond it, the shelter plaza churned with water and bodies.

The gate mechanisms had no power. The surge she had redirected from the broken tower district had found the lowest available route. Her sabotage had not merely exposed the Council’s sealed doors. It had sent the water toward them.

She climbed.

At the top of the hatch, she could hear the people inside the shelter pounding from the other side of the iron. The attendants were trying to open the gates by hand. The crowd outside had become a single animal of terror. Mara reached for the manual release and found the cable burned through.

A man on the steps saw her. “You said you could open it.”

She looked at him. He had blood on his forehead and a child’s red shoe caught in the laces of one boot.

“I’m trying.”

“You said you could.”

The water rose to the threshold.

Mara pulled until the cable cut her palms. It did not move. Behind the doors, the people inside screamed that the lower locks were buckling. The iron shuddered. Bolts jumped in their housings.

For years afterward, she remembered the Council as the voice that answered them: the guards refusing the corridor, the officials protecting the ridge, the hidden lists that had already decided whose lives could be spent. All of that was true. She had held the records. She had seen the schedules. She knew the city had built its safety upward and called the drowning districts acceptable.

But another truth waited beneath it.

She had cut the power.

She had made the network hungry enough to drain the shelter’s gates. She had sent the surge down the channel because she believed she could direct it. She had stood before the crowd and promised control with no more than a word.

The left gate tore loose first.

The people nearest it disappeared beneath the water. Mara saw the woman with the baby reach for the awning post. She saw the child’s red blanket open like a flag, then vanish. The right gate held for three breaths. Four. On the fifth, the hinges screamed.

Mara let go of the cable.

She did not order their deaths. She had not wanted the shelter to fill. She had wanted the doors opened, the records exposed, the city forced to look.

Yet wanting a different ending did not unmake the path she had built toward this one.

The water lifted her from the steps and carried her into the dark avenue. Behind her, the shelter lamps went out one by one.

She surfaced beside a toppled carriage and clung to its axle. The bells continued above the flood, immense and triumphant. For a moment she heard them as she had heard them before: her hand upon the city’s throat, making it speak.

Then she understood what she had wanted.

Not merely to reveal the catastrophe.

To command it.

She had wanted the flood to obey her more completely than the Council obeyed its own laws. She had wanted every tower, gate, current, and frightened citizen to become part of a design only she could see. The Council had made people expendable. She had believed that if she held the mechanism tightly enough, she could decide what their deaths meant.

The bells rang on.

Mara pressed her face against the carriage axle and vomited river water. When she raised her head, the shelter was gone behind a brown wall of tide.

For the first time, she did not call the dead evidence.

She called them people.

And because the word could not be used to move them, excuse her, or make the city obey, she had nowhere to put it except inside herself.

chapters.name: The Second Design
chapters.content:
The Second Design

The maintenance spine ended at a door that had not been on Oris’s fragments.

It stood twelve feet high, plated in new gray metal, its seams bright with sealant. Water moved beneath it with a slow, muscular pull. Someone had built the door recently, not to keep the flood out but to keep witnesses from seeing what had been put inside.

Mara laid her palm against the metal. It vibrated.

“Pressure?” Juno asked.

“Not yet,” Oris said. He leaned over his instrument case, pale beneath the blue wash of Vessa’s lamp. “The chamber beyond is holding a head of water. More than the original plans allow.”

Tomas lifted his route slate. “This door wasn’t on any Council survey.”

“Neither were the orders to burn the records,” Juno said. She had her rifle shouldered, muzzle aimed at the dark behind them. “We are collecting omissions.”

Ilya tightened the cloth around Mara’s temple. “You’re bleeding again.”

“I’m aware.”

“That wasn’t an invitation to be aware more forcefully.”

Mara almost answered. The old reflex rose—correct the tone, define the task, put every person back into a useful place. She swallowed it. The water beneath the door gave a deep, distant knock.

Vessa pointed to a narrow inspection hatch. “There.”

Oris’s fingers trembled as he opened it. Warm air breathed through the gap, carrying rust, oil, and the mineral stink of an enclosed sea. Beyond the hatch, a catwalk crossed a cavern large enough to swallow the market tower. Lamps hung at intervals along the rail, all new, all wired into a cable that disappeared upward.

And below them, the flood engine waited.

It was not a single machine but a city’s buried skeleton: pressure drums sunk into the rock, toothed wheels taller than houses, pipes vanishing into the black water, and six great channels branching away from the central cavern. The old engine had been built to distribute force, to let the surge spend itself across districts according to measured limits. Its purpose had been balance.

The new work had altered that purpose.

Steel collars encircled the six channels. Fresh diversion gates had been bolted into the old stone, each one angled toward the lower routes. Their faces bore white numbers and red Council seals. Three channels leading toward the upper city had been narrowed nearly shut. The remaining passages—South Reach, District Four, the drowned markets—stood open beneath raised gates.

Oris made a sound like a cough, though no breath followed it.

“They’re not repairing the engine,” he said. “They’ve made it selective.”

Mara descended the first ladder. Her boots struck the catwalk, and the whole chamber answered with a hollow ringing. She walked to the nearest control housing. Its casing was new, but the bolts had been driven through the old access plate, sealing the original manual release.

Tomas came after her. “What does selective mean?”

“Once the surge reaches the pressure drums, the upper gates close first. These remain open.” Oris pointed with a shaking hand. “The water will be routed through the lower districts. It will clear them.”

“Clear them for what?” Ilya asked.

On the far wall, someone had painted a development map over the damp stone. Elevated terraces were marked in gold. New roads crossed what had been the tide districts. Blocks of identical housing stood where the drowned market and South Reach had been. Along the lower margin, in the Council’s neat blue lettering, was written: RECLAIMED CIVIC EXPANSION.

Vessa stared at it. “They’ll call it a floodplain after they take the people out.”

“No,” Tomas said. He had gone very still. “They’ll call it protection.”

A speaker crackled overhead.

The voice that came through was calm, polished, and close enough to seem spoken beside Mara’s ear.

“Expedition team, acknowledge.”

Juno raised her rifle toward the ceiling. “Ardin.”

Mara looked at the black speaker grille. “You’ve been listening.”

“Monitoring,” said Councilor Sere Ardin. “There is a distinction, though I appreciate that your circumstances may make nuance difficult.”

“You built gates to drown the lower districts.”

A pause. Not surprise. Calculation.

“The engine is unstable. A controlled release through unoccupied containment zones is the only responsible course. The lower districts are already compromised by contamination, structural failure, and Bellmaker agitation. Evacuation will be orderly.”

Ilya laughed once, without humor. “There are people in those zones.”

“There are unauthorized populations in those zones,” Ardin replied. “The Council has prepared transport and labor allocation.”

Mara felt the chamber narrow around her. For one instant she saw the south shelter again: hands against the gates, mouths opening behind wire, the surge climbing the stairs. She had made the power fail. She had made the water choose a direction. The memory did not excuse Ardin. It removed the comfort of pretending that cruelty required only one author.

“Send us the order,” Mara said.

“Already transmitted.”

A strip of paper uncurled from the control housing. It was warm from the printer. Juno tore it free and read aloud.

“By authority of the Council, prisoner Mara Venn is to restore the upper regulation controls and stabilize the engine. Access to diversion gates, lower channels, and manual distribution assemblies is prohibited. Any attempt to alter the containment design will constitute breach of commutation and active sedition. Expedition personnel are authorized to restrain or terminate her.”

The last line seemed to remain in the air after Juno finished.

Tomas reached for the paper. “The commutation terms said success and compliance. They didn’t define compliance as leaving the city’s poorest districts to drown.”

“They didn’t need to,” Ardin said. “The terms were always conditional on Council determination.”

Mara turned toward the speaker. “So there was never a release.”

“Your sentence may be reviewed upon satisfactory completion of service.”

“Reviewed by whom?”

“By the authority that imposed it.”

The answer was so clean it became a blade. Mara looked down at the six gates. Her conditional freedom had been another chamber with a new door, another arrangement in which someone else controlled the release. She had recognized the mechanism in every other part of her life. She had still stepped inside.

“You wanted the Bellmaker,” she said.

“We wanted the engine repaired.”

“You wanted me standing beside it when the lower city disappeared. Then the broadcasts would say I had returned to my work.”

Ardin’s silence confirmed more than denial could have.

From somewhere high above, a relay clicked. One of the upper channels began to close. The metal gate descended with immense patience. In the lower channels, warning lamps came alive one after another—red, red, red—until the cavern glowed like a row of watching eyes.

Oris stumbled toward the nearest instrument panel. “They’ve begun charging the pressure drums.”

“How long?” Juno asked.

“Perhaps three hours. Less if they open the intake from the outer reservoir.”

“Can we stop it?” Tomas asked.

Oris looked at Mara, then away. “The upper controls can delay the cycle. They cannot change where the force goes.”

Ardin spoke again. “Mara, repair the regulator. Do that, and your conditional review remains available. Touch the lower assembly, and I will order the guards to seal the chamber with you inside it.”

Juno’s jaw tightened. “You don’t have guards here.”

“Not yet.”

The speaker went dead.

For several breaths no one moved. Water struck stone below, steady as a pulse.

Mara took the paper from Tomas and folded it once, precisely. Then again. The motion was familiar, almost soothing. In the Bastion she had counted objects because objects did not lie. One cup. One blanket. Four bolts in the door. A body could lie. A government could lie. Metal, under pressure, merely failed according to its design.

She put the order into her instrument case beside the breathing gauge and Tower Three’s casualty assessment.

Ilya watched her. “What are you doing?”

“Keeping the evidence.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” Mara said. “It’s the part I can answer without pretending I know what comes next.”

Vessa moved to the rail. Far below, one of the newly installed gates groaned higher. A current turned in the cavern, drawing scraps of insulation and rust toward the open lower channel.

“If they open all six,” she said, “the first wave will take the market tower.”

“And the refuge,” Tomas added.

Mara looked across the machinery. The old design had tried to divide pressure. The second design divided people instead. It was the same argument the Council had made before the first flood: some lives were infrastructure, some were obstruction, some were permitted to remain only while useful.

Her hands wanted the controls. They wanted sequence, leverage, a clean intervention. She could hear the old voice insisting that if she seized the machine first, she could force every other choice to follow. That voice had worn the shape of necessity once. It had sounded like courage while she connected the reserve charge.

She stepped away from the upper control panel.

“We do not repair their design,” she said.

Juno looked at her. “And we don’t simply break it.”

“No.” Mara faced the lower gates. “We learn exactly what they changed. We keep the engine from choosing for us while we find a way to keep the people alive.”

Tomas’s expression held anger, fear, and something that was not yet trust. “That sounds like a plan.”

“It is an investigation.”

“It sounds like a plan.”

Mara allowed herself one breath, then another. Not command. Not surrender. A measure of the space between them.

“Oris,” she said, “show me the manual releases. Vessa, find out whether the lower maintenance spine has another entrance. Juno, secure the catwalk and count every weapon. Ilya—”

Ilya raised an eyebrow.

Mara stopped. The old arrangement waited in her mouth, ready to assign. She looked at the medic’s tired face, at the hand protecting her left side, at Oris’s shaking shoulders and Vessa’s hooked pole.

“Tell me what you need,” Mara said.

Ilya’s surprise was brief but visible. “Light. Dry bandages. And for you to stop deciding that everyone else is equipment.”

Mara nodded.

Below them, the engine turned. The lower gates opened another fraction, and the buried sea began to gather itself for the city.

This time, Mara did not mistake the gathering for a command. It was a danger. It was a design. And it was not yet an order she had to obey.

chapters.name: A Monster’s Use
chapters.content:
## A Monster’s Use

The pressure drums spoke beneath the floor.

Not loudly. That was the worst of it. Their vibration traveled through the soles of Mara’s boots and climbed her bones, a patient knocking from something too large to be hurried. Each pulse made the lamps tremble in their brackets. Each tremor loosened another thread of water from the ceiling.

Oris knelt beside the engine case with one hand pressed to its brass housing. His face had gone the gray of old paper. “Two hours and forty minutes,” he said. “Perhaps less. The charge is uneven.”

“Can you stop it?” Juno asked.

“I can stop the upper regulators from opening.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“No.” Oris looked toward the black archway where the diversion spine disappeared. “I cannot stop the flood from choosing the channels already prepared for it.”

Mara unfolded the map across a crate. The paper had gone soft at the edges from damp, and the inked lines seemed to swim. Six diversion gates. Three narrowed channels to the upper city. Three lower channels left wide and hungry. The arrangement was not a failure. It was an argument made in iron: some lives were worth preserving because their land was worth preserving.

Her pencil rested over South Reach.

“If I reverse the first gate,” she said, “the pressure will shear the second.”

“Likely,” Oris said.

“And if I jam the second?”

“The surge backs into the chamber.”

“Then we open the upper channels.”

Tomas gave a short, humorless laugh. “Ardin’s channels.”

Mara looked at him. “The upper districts have people in them.”

“People the Council has decided are more useful alive.”

“That does not make them acceptable losses.”

“No.” Tomas’s eyes moved to the map. “But it makes the choice uglier, which is not the same as making it impossible.”

She knew the shape of the choice. Destroy the engine now and the pressure would break wherever it found weakness. The lower districts would drown before the refugees could be warned. Repair the upper controls and delay the cycle, perhaps long enough to move the market tower’s people, but leave the Council’s design intact. Or take control of the machinery, hold the gates closed, and make Ardin bargain in public before she released a single measure of water.

Leverage. The word entered her mind cleanly, almost pleasantly.

She could hear his voice through the speaker: conditional, subject to review, return her alive. She could make his city wait on her hand. She could force the Council to open the labor compounds, publish the ledgers, withdraw the patrols. She could require the commutation in ink, witnessed by every district. She could make them need her so badly that they would have to admit what she was.

The thought warmed her more than the lamps did.

Then she remembered the shelter doors. Not the pounding first, but the moment before it: her fingers on the control lever, the grid faltering under her command, the certainty that one more adjustment would make the whole city listen. She had wanted the catastrophe to obey her. The people behind the doors had not been leverage. They had been people.

Mara took her hand from the map.

“We do not use the engine to bargain,” she said.

Tomas watched her carefully. “You decided that quickly.”

“No. I have been deciding it for twelve years.”

A sound came from the maintenance stair. Vessa appeared with two survivors behind her, both carrying hooked poles and salvaged lamps. The woman in front was broad-shouldered and silver-haired, with a strip of blue cloth tied around her wrist. Mara recognized her from the market tower, though she had not learned her name.

“Vessa says you plan to go below,” the woman said.

“To the central chamber,” Mara replied.

“You plan to touch the gates.”

“We need to understand the manual releases.”

“Understand.” The woman’s mouth tightened. “That is what you said in the tower before you moved us like crates.”

Mara felt Juno turn toward her, but did not look away from the woman. “I was wrong to do that.”

The admission seemed to unsettle everyone more than an order would have.

Vessa stepped past the woman. “Her name is Anik. She keeps the tower records. She says the enclave has voted.”

“On what?” Tomas asked.

“On you,” Anik said to Mara.

The water dripping through the ceiling marked the silence.

Anik continued. “Some say we should put a bullet through your head and leave you here for the flood. Some say we should bind you to the engine and make you repair what you broke. Some say your knowledge is the only reason any of us might see another morning.”

Ilya, who had been changing Oris’s bandage, went still.

“And what do you say?” Mara asked.

“I say the Council wants you alive. That makes your life useful. It does not make it precious.”

Mara had heard variations of that judgment from wardens, prosecutors, and strangers who spat at the Bastion gates. Yet this was different. Anik did not need Mara to be a monster in order to hate her. She did not need the Council’s story. Her dead were sufficient.

“Why tell me?” Mara asked.

“Because if we go below, you will not command us.” Anik pointed at the map. “You will explain what you know. We will decide what to do with it.”

Mara almost smiled. There it was: the old world’s preferred arrangement. Let the condemned provide the key, then decide whether to keep the hand that held it.

But beneath that thought was another, less comfortable one. Anik was offering her exactly what she had denied others: knowledge without obedience.

“I agree,” Mara said.

Tomas’s head snapped toward her. “You agree to what?”

“To explain. To advise. Not to command.”

“Those are not the same thing when the water starts moving.”

“I know.”

“No, you know how to make an order sound like a necessity.”

The words struck with the accuracy of a thrown tool. Mara’s jaw tightened. “And you know how to turn silence into caution.”

Tomas flinched, though he covered it by bending over the route slate.

Juno stepped between them. “Enough.” Her voice carried the authority of the captain’s clasp even in the dripping chamber. “We have less than three hours and one route forward. If either of you wants to settle old accounts, do it while walking.”

“Before we walk,” Ilya said, “there is something else.”

She faced Juno. Her left hand rested against her ribs, protective and tired. “The guards at the Bastion. What were their orders?”

Juno did not answer at once.

Mara felt the room narrow. “You know?”

“I read the dispatch before we left.”

“Read it aloud,” Anik said.

Juno’s eyes went to the speaker grille, as if Ardin might be listening through the static. “The expedition was authorized to restrain Mara Venn if she obstructed the repair. If restraint was not possible, lethal force was permitted.”

Oris swore softly.

“And the return order?” Tomas asked.

Juno’s hand closed around her rifle strap. “Mara was to be returned alive whenever practical.”

“Whenever practical,” Ilya repeated. “Why?”

Juno looked at Mara. “Because the Council needs the Bellmaker.”

The phrase seemed to lower the temperature.

“They need a body for the story,” Juno said. “A living one is better. If the engine fails, they can display you. If it holds, they can say you were useful under supervision. Either way, people will be told that the monster was contained.”

Mara’s old belief rose to meet the words. Society relished monsters. It fed them to its children in lessons, to its frightened citizens in broadcasts, to its officials as proof that the machinery around them was innocent. A monster made every other hand clean.

But Anik’s expression complicated it. The survivors did not want the same monster for the same purpose. Some wanted punishment. Some wanted tools. Some wanted an answer to a practical problem. Their hatred was not a single appetite. It had names, faces, and disagreements.

The city did not secretly relish one monster.

The city had been taught to need one.

And she had made herself available.

“Then they will not have me as their symbol,” Mara said.

Tomas’s gaze hardened. “What will they have?”

“The truth, if we survive long enough to give it to them.”

“That is still a use.”

“Yes.” Mara picked up the map. “But not one they control alone.”

Vessa took the lamp from the younger survivor. “The lower maintenance spine begins behind the pressure drums. There is a crawlway, but it floods to the waist at high cycle.”

“Can the market tower be warned?” Ilya asked.

“Not from here. The old signal wire runs toward the central chamber. If we restore the relay, perhaps.”

“Perhaps,” Tomas said. “Everything is perhaps.”

Mara folded the map and slid it into her canvas case. “Then we take the route with the most information and the least irreversible damage.”

Anik gave a dry laugh. “That sounds like command.”

“It is a proposal.”

“Then we vote.”

They did, there among the engine’s trembling drums. The survivors voted to proceed. Juno voted with them, though she made clear that her rifle would answer any attempt to seize the gates. Ilya agreed on the condition that Oris would not be abandoned to increase their speed. Tomas agreed after making Mara repeat that no gate would be opened for leverage. Vessa agreed because the lower spine was the only path to the relay and the central chamber.

Oris raised one weak hand. “I agree because none of you understand the machinery.”

“Your vote is noted,” Juno said.

They began to prepare.

Mara distributed the lamps, then stopped herself before assigning positions. She held one out to Anik instead.

“Where do you want to walk?” Mara asked.

Anik studied her, suspicious of the question. “Near Vessa. We know the turns.”

“Then near Vessa.”

Tomas secured the route slate inside his coat. Ilya tightened Oris’s bandage and ordered him to use the rail whenever the passage narrowed. Juno checked every cartridge, then gave the recovered signal bead to one of the survivors.

“If I fall,” she said, “send this toward the tower. Three short, one long. It means armed help is coming.”

Mara looked at her. “That pattern belonged to the resistance.”

“It belongs to whoever uses it honestly,” Juno said.

The pressure drums struck again. Somewhere below, metal groaned against metal.

At the mouth of the crawlway, Tomas caught Mara’s arm. His grip was not hard, but it was not trusting either.

“If you see a way to save everyone,” he said, “you tell us before you act.”

“Yes.”

“If you see a way to punish the Council—”

“I tell you before I act.”

“And if telling us means losing the chance?”

Mara met his eyes. “Then I lose it.”

He released her, unconvinced. That was fair. Trust could not be demanded into existence by a sentence, even an honest one.

Mara entered the crawlway last. Behind her, the outer chamber remained lit, the mapless engine beating in the dark. Ahead, black water climbed the iron steps toward the central chamber and the gates that had already chosen their victims.

She placed one boot into it.

For twelve years she had counted every door that closed.

This time, she would not be the only person holding the key.

chapters.name: The Confession Tomas Kept
chapters.content:
## Chapter 17: The Confession Tomas Kept

After Mara disappeared into the Mirror Bastion, Tomas learned how quickly a city could turn a person into a boundary.

Her name was painted on walls beside the words FLOOD-MURDERER. Children were taught to make a bell with their hands and then crush it beneath their heel. The Council printed commemorative notices listing the dead beneath the heading Bellmaker Attack, as if one woman had stood at every gate, turned every pump, and chosen every body for the water.

Tomas read the notices in the records annex after midnight, when the lamps burned low and the clerks had gone home.

He read until the ink doubled.

Then he opened the maintenance book he had altered.

The original entries were still visible beneath the scraped pages. He had not been able to remove them cleanly. The paper remembered. A pressure mark where he had written unstable release assembly. A torn fiber where he had cut out the line naming the lock’s displacement. A smear of sealing wax over the date of his warning to Mara.

He had made the record incomplete.

He had also made it survivable.

That was the argument he repeated while the Council investigator waited outside the annex door.

If the book remained whole, the Council would burn the book and arrest every keeper who had ever touched it. They would destroy the evacuation ledgers. They would erase the tower diagrams. They would make the disaster entirely hers, but without leaving behind anything that might one day contradict them.

Tomas had preserved the fragments in a concealed drawer beneath the records table. He had copied the missing pages in his own hand and hidden them behind a false back in the archive wall. He had taken the Council position because access was the only protection he could think of.

He had told himself this was courage wearing an ugly coat.

It was also fear.

The investigator came in.

“Vale,” she said. “The Council wants a statement before dawn.”

“About what?”

“You were there.”

“So were hundreds of people.”

“You were with her.”

The investigator placed a prepared account on the table. It described Mara as the sole designer of the tower attack. It called the resistance a cult. It said the Council had acted without warning only because the Bellmaker’s followers had compromised the civic channels.

Tomas looked at the sentence about the channels.

“Where are the evacuation lists?” he asked.

The investigator’s expression did not change. “There were no lists.”

“I saw them.”

“You saw documents seized from a terrorist cell.”

“They named northern families and assigned routes.”

“Then you should be careful what you remember.”

She tapped the prepared statement. “Sign this, and you will be appointed to the reconstruction inquiry. Refuse, and you will be tried with the others.”

Tomas thought of his sister in the north quarter. He thought of the surviving tower keepers, hiding in rooms whose doors could be kicked open before breakfast. He thought of Mara below the court, waiting to hear whether he would say the lock had been unstable.

He signed.

The pen made a small, dry sound.

For twelve years, he would call that sound a compromise.

He began in the Council’s Department of Civic Continuity, where the dead were sorted into columns and the living into categories of usefulness. He was given a narrow office above the floodworks and assigned to investigate the resistance’s methods. He accepted because the position granted him access to maintenance orders, pump schedules, sealed testimony, and the records that had vanished from the trial.

At first he worked like a thief.

He copied diversion maps before they were revised. He memorized the names of clerks who signed relocation orders. He slipped carbon sheets beneath official forms and carried impressions home in the lining of his coat. He found that the Council had marked South Reach as acceptable inundation years before the bells. He found emergency routes reserved for elevated families, laborers ordered to remain at the pumps, and hospital corridors protected while the tide districts filled.

Every discovery gave him a reason to continue.

Every discovery also confirmed that he had chosen the Council’s roof while Mara had been left beneath the rain.

He told himself the difference was strategic. She had been condemned; he was free to gather proof. She was a symbol; he could move through the machinery that made symbols. If he exposed the scheme at the right moment, the truth would balance the scales.

Balance became his word for postponement.

He postponed sending the records to the surviving resistance. He postponed bringing them to the press. He postponed confronting the judges who had sealed them. Each delay had a reason. The evidence was not complete. The city was unstable. A premature accusation would let the Council dismiss everything as Bellmaker propaganda.

Meanwhile, Mara remained in the Bastion.

The Council’s version grew stronger with every year she was silent.

Tomas visited the Bastion twice under the title of investigator. The first time, he stood behind the mirror partition while Warden Pell brought Mara into the interview room. She had cut her hair close to her skull. Her hands rested on the table, palms down, as if keeping herself from rising through the floor.

She did not ask him whether he had altered the records.

She asked, “Did you tell them about the lists?”

Tomas had brought three copied pages in his satchel. He could have placed them between them. He could have said: I kept these. I was afraid. I chose myself and called it a method.

Instead he said, “The records are being reviewed.”

Mara smiled without amusement. “That is what people say when records are being buried.”

He asked whether she remembered the timing line. She answered every question precisely. She explained the charges, the tower sequence, the point at which the system became unstable. Her voice was calm enough to make the room feel colder.

“Tell them,” he said.

“Tell them what?”

“That you did not intend the deaths.”

“I have told them.”

“No. Tell them what you changed.”

Her eyes hardened. “You want a confession.”

“I want the truth.”

“You want the truth arranged so it can survive you.”

Pell struck the glass with his baton. “Interview concluded.”

Tomas stood, carrying the pages back out.

He had come to give her evidence and left with another accusation. He resented her for making it. He resented himself because it was accurate.

Years passed. The Council promoted him from investigator to senior examiner. He became useful in the way a knife was useful: quiet, narrow, and trusted to enter places other tools could not. He helped identify unauthorized engineers. He signed orders for searches. He learned how to ask questions that made frightened people contradict themselves.

He did not consider himself cruel.

Cruelty, he thought, was what the Council did openly. His own work was containment. Preservation. The gradual gathering of proof.

But sometimes, after an interrogation, he would see Mara’s face in the black reflection of a lift door and understand that the machinery did not care what name he gave his hand on the lever.

On the twelfth anniversary of the flood, he found the final ledger in a sealed sub-basement beneath the old pumpworks. It contained the original emergency route authorization from the night of the bells. The northern roads had been cleared before the first tower rang. The shelter corridors had been assigned by household rank. South Reach had not merely been neglected; it had been written into the plan as a place the city could afford to lose.

Tomas sat on the wet floor with the ledger open across his knees.

He saw again the tower, the charges, Mara’s face turned toward the rising sound. He remembered warning her. He remembered failing to stop her. He remembered the Council offering him a position because someone had to make the records legible, and understood that they had not chosen him despite his guilt but because of it.

He had preserved the evidence.

He had also preserved the lie.

His testimony at the trial had been incomplete, but not false. He had said Mara changed the plan. He had said she ignored the warning. He had refused to say she intended murder. He had mentioned withheld records, knowing the court would seal the mention and retain the accusation.

He had told himself that a partial truth was better than silence.

Now he wondered whether partial truth was simply silence with a witness standing beside it.

That night, Tomas returned to his office and took out the old maintenance copy. He laid it beside the ledger, then beside the evacuation orders, then beside the casualty assessment that gathered every death beneath Mara’s name.

The documents formed a neat little tribunal.

Mara had caused devastation. The Council had prepared to profit from it. Tomas had known enough to object and not enough—or not bravely enough—to pay the price of objecting. All three facts could stand together. None erased the others.

At dawn, a courier brought him an order from Ardin’s office. The flood engine had begun behaving erratically. A Council expedition would be sent into the drowned undercity. Tomas was to command it.

The assignment included a sealed directive: recover the engine, control Mara Venn, and preserve the Bellmaker narrative until the Council determined how best to use it.

Tomas read the directive twice.

Then he unlocked the drawer beneath his desk and placed the copied records inside a canvas case. He did not know whether he meant to expose the Council, save Mara, or merely keep from being the only person who knew how much of the story had been chosen.

He knew one thing.

If he brought the evidence to Mara as a weapon, he would still be deciding what she was permitted to say. If he told the city everything while she remained silent, the Council would call it manipulation, and perhaps they would be right. Her admission could not absolve the dead. It could not make his cowardice noble. But without it, even the truth would become another structure built around her—a new cage, with his hands on the hinges.

Tomas closed the case.

For twelve years he had believed that truth, properly preserved, would eventually balance the scales.

Now he understood that truth could be used like any other instrument. It could expose. It could condemn. It could force a living person into the shape most convenient for those who claimed to speak for the dead.

He would take the records into the undercity.

He would show Mara what he had kept.

And before he spoke for her again, he would make her speak for herself.

Outside, the first warning bell of the morning sounded over Veyr.

Tomas stood beneath it, listening to the note tremble through the walls, and felt no balance arrive.

Only a choice.
