chapters.name: The Flood Chamber
chapters.content:
## Chapter 18: The Flood Chamber

The lower maintenance spine ended at a door that had no handle.

Vessa found the seam by running her lamp along the wall. Anik and the others crowded behind her, their wet clothes steaming faintly in the cold machinery air. Beyond the door, something immense moved with the slow patience of an animal asleep beneath stone.

“Pressure,” Oris whispered. “The chamber is already drawing.”

Mara put her palm against the metal. It trembled once, then again, like a pulse.

Tomas came beside her. He carried the canvas case beneath his coat. For a moment he said nothing. Then he drew out a packet wrapped in oilskin and held it toward her.

“The copies,” he said. “Evacuation orders. The original route authorization. My altered maintenance records.”

Mara did not take them.

“You brought them this far.”

“I should have brought them to you twelve years ago.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No.” His fingers tightened on the packet. “It is the only answer I have.”

She accepted it. The paper was warm from his body. She slid the packet into her instrument case beside the Tower Three casualty assessment and Ardin’s order. Evidence accumulated weight. It did not become justice merely because it was carried.

Vessa pressed a lever hidden under the door’s rim. Locks withdrew somewhere in the wall.

The door opened onto darkness and water.

The central chamber was not a room so much as a hollowed mountain. A tidal cavern yawned beneath a domed roof, its black ceiling lost among ribs of iron and old masonry. Platforms crossed the void at different heights. Pressure drums, each taller than a house, revolved around a central shaft. Chains descended into the cavern and vanished below the rising surface. Far beneath them, seawater struck the rock with a sound like breathing through broken teeth.

The engine had been built around the tide, not against it. It listened to the water and answered by opening one throat or another.

Oris stared across the platforms. “There.”

Six gates surrounded the chamber, each set into a channel mouth. The new upper controls gleamed with recent brass. Below them, reached by ladders and narrow walks, were the old manual assemblies: counterweights, ratchets, release wheels, and cages where workers had once stood to reset the machinery by hand.

A red line of light crawled across the pressure gauge.

“How long?” Juno asked.

“Less than an hour before the first surge enters the chamber.” Oris coughed into his sleeve. “The upper regulators can slow the cycle. They cannot change its destination. To restart the balancing sequence, someone must reset the lower diversion gates while the chamber floods.”

“Someone,” Ilya said, “meaning?”

“Someone who can reach the wheels, understand the order, and remain alive.”

Mara counted the gates. One through six. Two channels angled toward the lower districts. Three narrowed toward the elevated reservoirs. The Council’s new design had not merely chosen a sacrifice. It had made the choice look like physics.

A clicking sound came from the door behind them.

Juno raised her rifle. “Down.”

The first shot struck the railing where Mara’s head had been. Metal screamed. Figures poured through the doorway in gray flood armor, their masks sealed, their weapons fitted with short-range bolts. Behind them came a second squad on the upper gantry. Council agents. Ardin had not sent guards to retrieve the expedition. He had sent men to close the chamber around it.

Vessa shouted. Anik shoved two survivors behind a pressure drum. A bolt punched through the lamp in a young man’s hand. Darkness swallowed half the platform.

“Back!” Juno fired twice. One agent fell into the water below. Another shot caught Juno high in the shoulder, spinning her against the rail. Her rifle clattered away.

“Juno!” Ilya moved toward her.

“Stay with Oris!” Juno snarled. Blood ran down her sleeve. “Keep the engineer breathing!”

Three survivors went down in the first exchange. One disappeared between the grating and the surge. Another lay facedown beside the dead lamp. The third was Anik’s brother, Senn, who had been carrying a coil of signal wire. Anik reached for him, but Vessa seized the back of his coat and dragged him behind cover as bolts struck the floor.

Mara felt the old command rise in her—not a thought, but a structure assembling itself. The chamber had positions. Heights. Choke points. The attackers had entered through the service door and occupied the upper gantry. The bell circuitry ran along the east wall, obsolete signal lines feeding the warning relays above. Six circuits. Six gates. A current through the old lines would trigger the magnetic locks on the maintenance cages.

She could make the chamber obey.

“Mara,” Tomas said, seeing her face. “Tell us.”

She pointed. “Vessa, take the west drum. Anik, keep the survivors low. Ilya, Juno’s wound is high but not arterial—bind it and get her behind the third brace. Tomas, with me to the relay cabinet.”

No one moved.

Mara forced herself to breathe. “This is a plan, not an order. If anyone has a better route, speak now.”

A bolt struck the stone beside Tomas.

“Make it fast,” he said.

They ran.

Mara reached the relay cabinet and tore away its corroded cover. The old bell wires were coated in salt, but the layout remained legible. She clipped her signal wire across two terminals, then used the restraint cable to bridge the ground. Above, a warning bell mechanism shuddered in the dark. It had no bell left, only a hammer and a housing, but the circuitry still remembered how to summon attention.

“On my mark,” she called. “Vessa, pull the west release. Anik, when the gate cage opens, drop the walkway ladder.”

“What will it do?” Anik shouted.

“Give us a wall.”

“And the agents?”

“It may trap them.”

May. The word steadied her more than certainty would have.

Mara struck the contact.

The chamber rang without sound. Every old relay fired at once. Iron cages slammed down around the maintenance ladders. A counterweight released with a roar, dropping through the floor and wrenching the west gate half-shut. The upper gantry buckled as a ladder unfolded across it, trapping two agents behind a lattice of bars.

Vessa pulled the release wheel. Water burst through the west channel, throwing three armored figures from their feet. One vanished into the black below. Another caught the rail and hung there, kicking. Anik cut the rail with a stolen tool. The agent fell.

The surviving attackers broke formation. Juno, pale and furious, retrieved her rifle with her good hand and fired from behind the brace. Tomas shot the leader through the mask seam. The last two retreated toward the door, only to find the magnetic lock engaged. The pressure surge struck the threshold. The agents were swept outward into the spine.

For several seconds there was only water, ringing metal, and breath.

Then Oris cried out.

He was on the lower platform beside the first gate, separated from the others by a widening sheet of water. The path behind him had folded when Mara triggered the counterweight. His tool case floated away. One hand clutched the gate wheel; the other pressed against his ribs.

“The reset sequence!” he called. “I need the marks from the original assembly!”

Mara looked across the chamber. The access bridge to Oris was already dipping beneath the tide. If she opened the north cage, the pressure would expose the lower walkway for twelve seconds. Enough time to reach him. Not enough time to bring everyone back.

“Leave him,” Juno said, understanding the calculation. “We can reset from here.”

“No,” Ilya said.

Mara had already lifted her hand toward the relay cabinet.

The old pattern spread before her: release north, lock west, transfer current, sacrifice the lower walk. Oris was one component in a system whose failure would drown thousands. The arithmetic was clean. The arithmetic had always been clean.

She touched the first terminal.

Ilya crossed the platform and slapped her hand away.

“Do not.”

Mara stared at her.

“I can open the cage,” Ilya said. “You can get to Oris. But you cannot trap him there because the plan becomes prettier without him.”

“The chamber will flood.”

“It is already flooding.”

“People will die if the sequence fails.”

“People have already died.” Ilya’s voice broke, but she did not lower it. “Senn is dead. Vessa’s people are dead. Juno is bleeding. Oris is drowning. You keep saying keeping everyone alive is the purpose, but every time the mechanism asks for a piece, you start looking at us like pieces on your board.”

The words struck deeper than the old accusations because they were not shouted by an enemy. They came from someone who had watched Mara pull Oris from poison water, watched her wait for survivors at the service hatch, watched her try and fail to become different by naming the failure.

Mara looked at the gate wheel in Oris’s hands.

Then she turned to the others.

“Vessa,” she said, “can you hold the west release?”

“Yes.”

“Anik, can you reach the lower ladder without crossing the exposed rail?”

“With a line.”

“Tomas, connect the relay only when I tell you. Juno, cover the south gantry. Ilya, stay with me. We bring Oris back before the second reset.”

Juno’s mouth tightened. “That is not the safest plan.”

“No,” Mara said. “It is the plan that includes him.”

They moved together.

Anik threw the signal line across the gap. Vessa braced it around the drum. Mara clipped herself to the cable and stepped onto the trembling bridge with Ilya behind her. Water rose over their boots. Below, the tidal cavern opened and closed in slow black breaths.

Oris had begun turning the wheel. Each rotation released a shower of sparks and drove the old gate another inch toward alignment.

“Three marks!” he shouted. “Then the lower latch!”

Mara reached him as the bridge gave a long metallic groan. She seized his harness.

“Can you walk?”

“Insultingly, yes.”

They crossed back one at a time, Ilya behind them, Anik hauling the line. A new surge struck the chamber. The bridge dropped. Mara’s feet left the grating, and for one suspended instant Oris hung between her and the dark.

She pulled until the restraint cable cut her palms.

Ilya caught Oris’s arm. Together they dragged him onto the platform.

“Now!” Mara shouted.

Tomas completed the circuit. The six gates groaned in sequence—not the Council’s selective pattern, but the beginning of the engine’s original balance. Water changed direction below them. The pressure gauge faltered, then held.

No one cheered.

Juno leaned against the brace, blood soaking her sleeve. Vessa knelt beside the dead. Anik held the empty coil of wire against his chest. Oris lay gasping while Ilya pressed both hands to his ribs.

Mara stood at the relay cabinet with her burned fingers curled inward.

The chamber had not obeyed her. It had nearly taken Oris because she had asked it to. The difference mattered less than she wanted, and more than she deserved.

Ilya looked up at her.

“Next time,” she said, “you tell us before the board is drawn.”

Mara nodded.

Beyond the platforms, the flood engine began to turn.

And somewhere beneath the city, the tide answered.

set.description: Ilya is in the central chamber beside Oris on the main platform with her medical kit, treating Oris’s ribs and preparing to stabilize Juno’s shoulder. Her immediate goal is to protect the surviving refuge people and help complete the balancing sequence without abandoning anyone unnecessarily.

set.name: Anik
set.description: Anik is in the central chamber with the surviving helpers, carrying his hooked tools and the signal line after his brother Senn was killed in Ardin’s attack. He helped rig the line and rescue route across the failing lower bridge, remains grieving and furious, and is committed to protecting the survivors and assisting with the remaining manual gate work while judging Mara by her actions rather than the Council’s story.

The expedition entered the flood engine’s central tidal chamber, where Oris identified the six manual diversion assemblies and explained that restarting the original balancing sequence required resetting them during the flood.

Ardin’s agents attacked the central chamber, killing several survivor helpers and wounding Juno; the survivors and expedition trapped or drove off the attackers using the old bell circuitry and maintenance cages.

Mara’s relay trap opened the west channel and began the original balancing sequence, but its counterweight collapse stranded Oris on a flooding lower platform until Mara, Ilya, and the survivors rescued him.

Ilya confronted Mara for treating people as interchangeable pieces in her tactical calculations, and Mara thereafter made the rescue plan collectively, requiring the group to agree before completing the relay connection.

The expedition must complete the original balancing sequence by resetting the remaining diversion gates before the next surge, while preserving a survivable route for the lower districts and market-tower refuge.
Ilya and the group must stabilize Juno’s shoulder wound and keep Oris alive while the chamber continues flooding and the remaining gates are reset.

chapters.name: The Just Flood
chapters.content:
## Chapter 19: The Just Flood

The engine turned, but it did not yet choose a direction.

Its pressure drums revolved around the central shaft with a slow, grinding authority. Below the platform, water climbed the black walls of the tidal cavern. Each ascent erased a little more of the old masonry. The chamber smelled of salt, hot iron, and the copper tang of Juno’s blood.

Oris lay on his back while Ilya bound his ribs. He tried to count the rotations aloud and lost the number twice. Vessa and Anik had dragged the dead behind the west drum, away from the rising water. No one had enough breath left to mourn properly. The chamber allowed only tasks.

Mara stood over the gauges.

The first balancing gate had moved into position. The second had begun to answer. A thin green line, nearly hidden beneath the Council’s newer brass indicators, appeared along the old control face. It ran upward, then divided.

“Wait,” Oris said.

Mara bent closer. “What?”

“The return channel.” His voice was rough with pain. “The original system has a counterflow. I thought the lower plans were missing it. They weren’t missing it. They buried it.”

He pointed with a trembling hand.

The green line passed through the six gate symbols and ended at a small wheel beneath a plate stamped with the old civic seal. Mara scraped away salt with her pencil knife. Underneath, an arrow emerged. It curved away from the lower districts, away from the markets and the drowned tide wards, and toward the high reservoirs beneath North Rise.

She knew the reservoirs. Everyone in Veyr did. They sat under the elevated city like buried lakes, protected by double walls and staffed pump houses. Their overflow channels fed ornamental canals, private gardens, and the cisterns of the upper wards. During the old flood, the Council had protected them while the tide districts went under.

Oris swallowed. “If we open the return channel, the pressure will reverse through the new diversion design.”

“Reverse how?” Tomas asked.

“Instead of sending the surge through South Reach, it will push up into the elevated reservoirs. The new gates have narrowed everything toward the lower channels. But the old counterflow can force the water back.”

Mara looked at the map fixed to the control housing. Blue enamel marked the protected districts. Red marked the channels the Council had designated for inundation. With the return wheel engaged, the colors seemed to change places without moving.

The upper city would flood.

For one clean instant, the thought entered her like a breath held too long.

She saw North Rise under water. Saw the polished bridges vanish, the Council halls split open, the houses with their dry kitchens and heated floors filling from below. She imagined Ardin standing at a window while the tide climbed past his waist. Imagined the protected citizens pounding on gates they had once ordered sealed. Imagined them learning, in their bodies, what a lower district meant when the water arrived.

The chamber’s machinery gave a deep, approving thud.

Mara placed her hand on the return wheel.

“Open it,” Anik said.

His grief had made his face older. “Let them have the flood they built for us.”

Vessa looked from him to the map. “If it takes North Rise, the pressure may break the whole upper wall. It could run back through every channel.”

“Then they’ll have to choose whether to save us,” Anik said.

“No,” Mara replied.

The word surprised them, including her.

She turned the wheel a fraction. It resisted, then shifted. A vibration moved through the platform.

Tomas caught her wrist. “Don’t.”

She looked at his hand until he released it.

“You have an objection,” she said. “Make it one.”

“The return channel is not a punishment lever.”

“It is an engineering solution.”

“It sends a surge toward houses because those houses belong to people who were protected.”

“People were sent toward ours.”

“Yes.” Tomas’s face tightened. “That is what the Council did.”

Mara laughed once. It came out as a cough. “You’ve found the distinction now?”

His eyes moved to the canvas case at her feet, where the copied records rested beside the casualty assessment. “I found it late.”

“Late enough to sign their account. Late enough to let them call me the sole architect. Late enough to wear their seal for twelve years while you collected papers that could have saved no one.”

“I know.”

“No, you know the shape of the sentence. You don’t know the weight of it.”

“I know I allowed it.”

“You allowed me to carry it.”

The engine groaned. Far below, a gate slammed against its housing. The green line on the old panel brightened. Pressure was building faster than Oris had predicted.

Tomas stepped between Mara and the wheel, not quite blocking it. “I want forgiveness.”

The admission seemed to empty the air around them.

Juno, propped against the brace, opened one eye. Ilya paused with a strip of cloth in her hands. Even Anik stopped working the signal line.

Tomas continued. “I want you to say that what I did was survivable. That fear made it necessary. That I preserved the records, and that means I was not simply a coward who chose his life over yours.”

Mara’s palm still rested on the wheel. Its teeth pressed into her burned skin.

“You want me to absolve you.”

“Yes.”

“And you think confessing is the same as paying.”

“No. I think confession is the first thing I owe.”

The answer had no defense in it. That made it harder to strike.

He looked toward the dark water. “But my guilt does not give me the right to drown North Rise. Neither does yours give you the right to drown South Reach again. We don’t get to choose who must die because we are ashamed of the choices we already made.”

Mara felt the old philosophy rise to meet him. Everyone wanted a monster. Everyone needed one person to stand in the place where the city’s appetite could not be seen. Tomas wanted her guilt purified into a moral instrument. The Council had wanted her guilt made useful. Even the survivors, in their anger, wanted a shape they could point at.

And she wanted, terribly, to be the hand on the wheel.

“If I don’t reverse it,” she said, “the Council’s design continues. The lower districts are already marked. We save the people who were always going to be saved and call that balance.”

“We interrupt the design,” Tomas said. “We don’t inherit it.”

“How?”

“By keeping the gates open long enough to split the surge. By taking the loss where the machinery makes it unavoidable, not where vengeance makes it satisfying.”

“Those are the same thing to the dead.”

“Yes.” He met her eyes. “Which is why we do not make more of them to prove we remember the first.”

The phrase struck the place beneath her ribs where memory had lived for twelve years without a name. Shelter doors. Hands against metal. Her own current line sparking blue in the dark. The certainty that if she commanded the catastrophe, it would become an argument instead of a disaster.

She had wanted the city to learn. She had also wanted the city to kneel.

Oris pushed himself onto one elbow. “There may be a third configuration.”

Ilya shoved him back down. “There may be a fourth broken rib.”

“Listen,” he wheezed. “The return channel has three shutters. We don’t need to open all of it. If we feather the first, the surge can be divided between the upper reservoirs and the old floodplain.”

“Which still floods,” Vessa said.

“Part of it. Not the whole lower spine. But the manual shutters must be held at different tensions. The engine won’t do it alone.”

Mara studied the controls. Three shutters. Six gates. A network of hands, timing, and risk. No single lever that transformed justice into arithmetic.

“Who can reach them?” she asked.

“Vessa and Anik can reach the west and south assemblies. Tomas and I can—” Oris coughed. “I can direct. Not walk.”

“I’ll take the north assembly,” Mara said.

Tomas nodded. “And the return wheel?”

She looked at it. The polished houses of North Rise glimmered in her imagination, already drowning.

“We open the first shutter only,” she said. “Enough to break the Council’s pressure pattern. Not enough to turn the upper city into a target.”

Anik’s expression hardened. “You’re saving them.”

“We’re saving who we can.”

“That’s what they said when they closed the south shelter.”

Mara flinched. “Then watch me. If I start calling people necessary losses, stop me.”

Anik held her gaze for a long moment. “I will.”

Juno gave a strained breath that might have been approval. “Good. Because I can’t chase you with one arm.”

The next surge struck.

The platform lurched. Water exploded through the lower channels, black and white under the work lamps. The old gauges spun toward their red limits. Somewhere above, the city’s buried foundations answered with a long crack.

“Positions!” Mara shouted, then stopped herself. “Positions—if you agree.”

“Agreed,” Vessa said.

Anik lifted the signal line. “Agreed.”

Tomas checked the relay slate. “Agreed.”

Ilya tightened the bandage over Juno’s shoulder. “Move.”

Mara took the north route as the chamber flooded around them. The return wheel remained closed, but she kept one hand near it, feeling the engine’s pressure through the metal.

Not a weapon, she told herself.

Not an answer.

Only a machine, and the people who would decide together what it could be allowed to do.

Behind her, Tomas began calling the timing marks. His voice shook, but it did not command. One by one, the others answered.

The flood rose toward the gates.

And Mara, for the first time, did not ask whether the city deserved to be saved. She asked who was still within reach.

chapters.name: The Broadcast
chapters.content:
## Chapter 20: The Broadcast

The first voice came through the engine walls.

It was Mara’s voice, clear as a bell struck in an empty room.

“Citizens of Veyr,” it said. “The Bellmaker has resumed her campaign. The lower districts are under deliberate attack. Any obstruction of the Council’s engineers will be treated as collaboration. Remain in your homes. Await authorized evacuation.”

Mara stopped with one boot on the north assembly ladder.

Below her, the tidal chamber shuddered. Water surged through the grates, climbed the braces, and flung a skin of spray across the lamps. The voice continued, using the measured pauses she had once taught herself in the Bastion: four breaths between warnings, a half-second emphasis on words meant to lodge in frightened minds.

“I have chosen this flood. I accept the deaths that follow. The upper city will not be safe while I remain free.”

Oris made a sound between a cough and a curse. “That isn’t a live relay.”

“No,” Tomas said. He was bent over the slate, one hand gripping the rail. “It’s a prepared recording.”

Mara knew the cadence. She had heard it in court transcripts, in prison lessons, in the civic announcements that preceded her meals. Her own voice had been assembled from old testimony, intercepted messages, and the statement she gave after the arrest, when her mouth was split and her mind was still full of water.

Ardin had found a way to make the dead version of her speak.

The broadcast rolled outward through the buried conduits. The engine’s signal coils woke one after another, sending the recording into Veyr’s surviving towers. Even beneath the chamber, Mara felt the network take hold: a vibration in the metal, a thin electrical whine behind the water’s roar.

Then other sounds entered the transmission.

Screams. Shattering glass. A crowd chanting for the Bellmaker’s blood.

Tomas turned the slate toward her. Its cracked screen showed signal returns from the elevated districts. North Rise had begun to riot. The Council’s statement had reached the protected wards before the flood did. Families were dragging furniture against doors. Shopkeepers were breaking open civic armories. Patrols were forming at the bridges, their orders blinking across the relay map.

Below the red line that marked the lower districts, whole neighborhoods had gone dark.

“The patrols are leaving,” Tomas said. “Ardin is pulling them back to the upper roads.”

“Leaving for what?” Vessa called from the west assembly.

“To protect the people who can still complain,” Anik answered.

A new message flashed on the slate. AUTHORIZED UNITS: WITHDRAW FROM SOUTH REACH. SECURE NORTH RISE. DISREGARD UNREGISTERED REFUGEES.

Mara’s fingers tightened around the ladder.

The Council had made the choice openly now. No sealed order, no hidden map, no polite phrase about containment. The lower districts were to be abandoned, and her voice would carry the blame ahead of the water.

“Can you cut it?” she asked Tomas.

“Not from here. Ardin has the main signal chamber.”

“Then we take it.”

“The pressure cycle—”

“Can the old network still carry a voice?”

Tomas studied the slate. “If we route through the engine’s civic coils. The coils were built to transmit flood warnings. But the Council has isolated the lower repeaters.”

“Open them.”

“That would expose the chamber’s position.”

“They already know where we are.”

“No. Ardin knows where the engine is. He doesn’t know which manual assemblies we’re using.”

Mara looked at the signal wire running from Anik’s hands to the relay housing. “Then give him something else to follow.”

Anik stared at her. “You want to bait the signal?”

“I want every channel.”

The words came quickly, before she could shape them into a command. They were not the same thing. A selective transmission would be easy. She could send the evacuation ledgers to North Rise and the final-flood plans to the lower districts. She could tell each population the truth most likely to make it turn against Ardin. She could place herself at the center again, choose the sequence, choose the wound, choose the version of justice that would produce the greatest obedience.

The old Mara would have called that strategy.

The old Mara had called many things by their cleanest names.

Oris lifted his head. “Every surviving coil means less power for the gate timing.”

“Then we use the power once,” Mara said. “No reply, no correction, no control after the release.”

Tomas understood first. “A single open transmission.”

“Everything goes out.”

“Everything?”

“The ledgers. The diversion maps. Ardin’s order. The casualty assessment. The final-flood plan.” Her mouth had gone dry. “And my account.”

Ilya looked over from Juno. “Your account of what?”

Mara climbed down from the ladder. Water had reached the second rung. “The first flood.”

No one spoke for a moment except the false Mara, still promising death through the walls.

Vessa’s lamp swung toward her. “If you tell them only what the Council did, they’ll make you a martyr.”

“Yes.”

“If you tell them what you did, they may use it to excuse everything else.”

“Yes.” Mara looked at the gathering faces—the wounded, the furious, the survivors who had not yet decided whether to trust her hands. “They may do both. I can’t choose what they make of it.”

Anik’s jaw worked. “Then say Senn’s name.”

“I will.”

“And the others.”

“All the names we have.”

“Not just the numbers.”

“Not just the numbers.”

Tomas moved to the relay housing. “The old civic coils require a synchronizing phrase.”

Mara almost smiled. “Three short. One long.”

The resistance signal. The signal the Council had copied to summon patrols. A pattern that had once meant gather, listen, act. Now it would open every surviving ear in Veyr.

“Can you make the connection?” she asked.

“With help.”

Mara set her instrument case beside him and opened it. The casualty assessment lay atop the papers, its corners damp. Beneath it were the evacuation lists, the labor-compound orders, Tomas’s copied maintenance book, and Ardin’s command forbidding access to the diversion system. Evidence gathered like kindling. Evidence that could burn the lie, if anyone survived long enough to hear it.

She handed Tomas the signal wire. “Route it through the north coil first.”

“That will draw the patrols.”

“Good.”

He hesitated. “Mara.”

“What?”

“When the channel opens, there may be no way to stop it.”

She looked toward the control face. The first return shutter trembled under the pressure. North Rise remained a possibility, not yet a target. The lower floodplain waited beneath them, already receiving more water than it could bear. Every decision pressed against the next one.

“I know,” she said. “That is why I’m doing it.”

They worked without hierarchy. Anik crawled beneath the relay deck to splice the line. Vessa braced the west assembly while calling out the depth of the water. Ilya shouted for clean cloth and forced Oris to remain seated as he calculated the coil load. Juno, pale and sweating, used her good arm to hold the timing slate against the brace.

The false confession ended.

For one breath, the city was silent.

Then Ardin’s voice replaced it, amplified and cold. “Mara Venn has attempted to seize the flood engine. All loyal citizens are instructed to resist Bellmaker agents. Security forces will withdraw from the contaminated districts at once.”

A door slammed somewhere above. The chamber lights flickered.

“Now,” Tomas said.

Anik struck the relay key three times. A fourth pulse followed, longer than the others.

The signal went out.

Mara heard the first repeaters catch it in sequence: a tower near the drowned market, a civic mast at South Reach, a damaged station beyond the old tram line. Then, faintly, the upper network answered. The transmission spread through Veyr in overlapping waves, breaking through Ardin’s command channel and filling every speaker that still had power.

Mara stepped to the microphone.

Her own recorded voice whispered underneath the live circuit, trying to continue its confession. Tomas cut the loop. The false Mara vanished.

“This is Mara Venn,” she said.

Her voice shook. She let it.

“I am speaking through every channel still open because no district should receive only the truth that makes it useful to someone else.”

The engine thundered. In North Rise, she imagined polished rooms going quiet. In the lower wards, people gathering around dead radios, broken tower horns, any device that could carry a human sound.

“The Council has ordered the lower districts abandoned. Its final-flood plan directs the next surge through South Reach, District Four, and the drowned markets so that those lands can be cleared for elevated development. I am releasing the orders now. I am releasing the evacuation ledgers, which show that Veyr has repeatedly protected the upper districts by denying routes, pumps, and warning time to the lower ones.”

Tomas fed the documents into the transmitter. The coils flashed. Somewhere beyond the chamber, public screens and tower lamps began displaying pages of copied text.

“Listen carefully,” Mara continued. “The Council did not cause the first flood alone. It built the unequal walls. It prepared escape for some and confinement for others. It sealed rescue corridors. It concealed the dead. It has done the same during this flood.”

Her breath caught.

“But I caused devastation too.”

The words entered the network without ornament.

“Twelve years ago, I connected a reserve charge to the warning towers after I was warned that the oldest maintenance lock was unstable. I chose a simultaneous ringing because I believed terror would force the city to listen. The tower fell. A chemical reservoir ruptured. Power failed to the shelter gates. Water reached people who had trusted the warning system, and many of them died.”

Ilya lowered her eyes. Anik’s hand stopped on the wire.

“I did not order every death. I did not design the Council’s evacuation scheme. Those facts are both true. Neither cancels the other.”

She opened the casualty assessment.

“I will name the dead recorded here. Tower Three keeper Halren Doss. The shelter wardens—Mira Pell, Jon Saye, Kett Aru. Senn of the market tower. Lio, Vessa’s brother. The children listed only as numbers because the Council could not be bothered to learn their names. I will read every name we have, and where we have none, I will say that the record failed them.”

She began.

Names moved through the chamber and out across the city. Some belonged to resistance workers. Some to shelter families. Some to patrols and engineers. Some were names Mara had never seen before. She read them all, stumbling over spellings, correcting herself when Tomas checked the ledger. No music accompanied them. No Council seal. No declaration of victory.

At last she said, “The engine is failing. We are attempting to divide the surge rather than send it wholly toward the lower districts or reverse it into North Rise. That choice will not save everyone. We do not know yet who can be saved. I will not call the dead necessary. I will not call vengeance justice. If we live, the records remain public, and so does my testimony.”

The water struck the north assembly with a force that threw her against the rail. Pain burst through her temple. The microphone shrieked.

“Mara!” Tomas shouted.

She caught the rail and returned to the transmitter.

“Hold the gates,” she said, not as an order but as a plea carried into every district. “Open what you can. Do not abandon the people nearest you. If a patrol has been told to withdraw, decide whether that order protects citizens or property. You have heard the truth. You must decide what to do with it.”

She released the key.

The transmission continued to carry the documents, the names, the raw hiss of the flooding chamber. No one could edit it now. No one could make her voice say only what served them.

Far above, bells began to ring—not in unison, not under one hand, but from different districts answering one another through the storm.

Mara put both hands on the north wheel.

“Your pressure is rising,” Oris said.

“I know.”

“Then turn.”

She looked once at Tomas. He nodded. At Anik. He was still watching her. At Ilya, Vessa, Juno, and the dark water climbing around the machinery.

Then Mara feathered the shutter open, and let the city hear the engine choose no single master.
