chapters.name: Every Channel
chapters.content:
The confession did not travel like a message. It traveled like a crack in glass.

For twelve years, Veyr had been given one face to hate. The Bellmaker appeared on broadsheets with a narrow jaw, a black coat, and eyes drawn too calm for a murderer. Children learned the rhyme before they learned the names of the drowned. In the upper districts, bells were still forbidden after sunset, lest someone imitate her signal. In the tide districts, where the dead had no monuments, people had learned to spit whenever the Council spoke her name.

Now her voice entered kitchens, guard posts, shelter rooms, patrol skiffs, and the sealed apartments of North Rise.

I connected the charge, Mara said. I was warned. I chose to continue.

The old civic coils shuddered around the chamber. Their copper throats gave her words a human roughness, carrying the cough beneath them and the fatigue that made each breath sound borrowed. The sound passed through the surviving towers, through relay bells, through the emergency lamps wired to public speakers. It reached places the Council had never intended to hear one another.

At the market tower, Vessa stood on the third landing with one hand against the cracked wall. Below her, the refuge had gone silent. Children who had been crying over the dead helpers stopped. An old man lowered the knife he had been sharpening. Lio’s name had already been spoken. Mara had named him without asking whether the living were ready to hear it.

“She’s doing it,” someone whispered. “She’s making herself the center again.”

Vessa looked toward the black water visible through the broken windows. “No,” she said, though she did not know if it was true. “She’s making room for the bodies.”

A woman near the stairwell laughed once, harshly. “A confession broadcast by a prisoner, using stolen Council channels? That’s another performance.”

“Then why release the records?” Anik asked. He held the signal wire against the relay post, fingers trembling with exhaustion. “Why put her own name beside theirs?”

The woman had no answer. Across the city, no one did.

In North Rise, Council families crowded around polished receivers while patrol commanders shouted for the signal to be cut. The first ledgers appeared as columns of light on public walls: names, carriage assignments, protected routes, districts marked for abandonment. A child read aloud the line identifying South Reach as acceptable inundation. His mother slapped the receiver dark. The image remained glowing on the wall behind it.

“Forgery,” said a magistrate.

“Bellmaker theater,” said another.

But below their voices, Mara continued. She described the shelter gates. She described the pounding from the other side. She said she had once turned that pounding into an argument against the Council, because an argument was easier to bear than the knowledge that her own sabotage had cut the power. She did not call herself innocent. She did not call herself the only guilty one.

That refusal unsettled the city more than any accusation could have.

In a guard station beside East Rise, Juno’s fellow officers heard the order to withdraw from the undercity and secure the elevated approaches. They heard the commander repeat it, then heard the final-flood plan underneath, where the lower districts were shaded in red and the phrase controlled loss appeared beside them.

Sergeant Dain read the order twice. His mouth tightened.

“Move,” said the patrol captain. “We leave through the north sluice.”

A young guard looked at the map. “My sister is in District Four.”

“Then she should have evacuated when instructed.”

“There was no instruction,” the guard said. “Not to us.”

The captain drew his pistol. “That is an order.”

Dain struck the pistol aside. The shot went into the ceiling, showering the room with plaster. For a breath, everyone stood in the dust, listening to Mara’s voice come through the receiver.

I did not know everyone I killed. They knew the warning was mine. They trusted it.

Dain turned to the others. “We don’t secure North Rise.”

The captain stared at him. “You’re committing mutiny.”

“Yes,” Dain said. “Open the south stores. Take the rescue boats. Anyone who wants to come with us comes. Anyone who wants to keep following that order can explain it to the people we leave behind.”

One by one, the guards lowered their weapons.

The mutiny began in three stations and became twelve before the Council could name it. Some officers joined because they had family below. Some because they had seen the ledgers. Some because the order was finally too naked to obey without calling obedience by its proper name. Others refused, shouting that Mara had manipulated them with a staged confession. Both groups heard the same broadcast. That was the wound: no authorized interpretation arrived to close it.

In the tidal chamber, the water reached Mara’s ribs.

She kept both hands on the return wheel. Each time the mechanism lurched, pain flashed through her palms and up her arms. The north shutter had begun to catch. Oris called figures from the platform, his voice ragged beneath Ilya’s commands to breathe. Vessa and Anik answered from their assemblies. The old engine complained in tones that resembled bells heard underwater.

“Pressure is climbing on west!” Anik shouted.

“Do not chase it,” Mara called back.

“That is what the Council said before they drowned us!”

“I know.”

The answer traveled through the chamber, not through the coils. Anik looked over his shoulder. For an instant his face held the old fury, then the wheel beneath him kicked and he bent to it.

Ilya had tied a strip of cloth around Juno’s shoulder. It was already dark with blood. Juno’s good hand gripped the brace, keeping her upright.

“Your guard stations are moving,” Tomas said. He was crouched at the relay housing, one ear pressed to a cracked receiver. “Dain has opened the south stores. Two patrols are heading toward the lower sluices.”

“Can they get here?”

“If Ardin doesn’t shut the routes.”

As if summoned by the name, every speaker in the chamber clicked. Ardin’s voice replaced Mara’s, clean and amplified.

“Citizens of Veyr, the prisoner is attempting to prolong the attack. Do not trust the records. They have been altered by Bellmaker sympathizers. The Council will restore order.”

Mara felt the familiar temptation rise through her exhaustion: seize the coil, drown him beneath a greater voice, make the city hear only what she knew. Control returned in the shape of an emergency. It was almost comforting.

Tomas looked at her. He knew the expression.

“Don’t answer him by becoming him,” he said.

She turned the wheel another fraction. “I’m not answering.”

The receiver on his knee spat a burst of static. Then a guard’s voice broke through.

“Signal chamber access sealed. Councilor Ardin is present. He’s ordering the upper relays cut.”

Tomas rose too quickly and nearly fell. Ilya caught his elbow.

“Where are you going?”

“To stop him.”

“You can’t walk there.”

“Then I’ll crawl.”

Mara watched him look toward the narrow maintenance stair climbing from the chamber. Twelve years ago, he had gone away from the tower while she connected the charge. Twelve years ago, he had chosen a different kind of survival. Now he was leaving the gate at the moment it demanded every hand.

“Go,” she said. “But don’t decide for us what happens while you’re gone.”

His eyes met hers. “I won’t.”

The stair was half flooded. Tomas climbed with one hand on the rail and the other holding the copied maintenance book against his chest. Behind him, two mutinous guards emerged from the lower passage, their uniforms scraped and their weapons held down.

“Dain sent us,” one said. “We know the relay route.”

“Then keep up,” Tomas replied.

They reached the signal chamber through a service hatch above the civic coils. Ardin stood beneath the main lens, surrounded by dead monitors and a web of lit control lines. He had removed his formal coat. Without it, he looked smaller, a tired man holding a city together with clenched fingers.

“You,” Ardin said.

Tomas closed the hatch behind him. “Me.”

“You have betrayed the Council.”

“I signed your lie.” Tomas’s voice was quiet. “I copied your orders. I let her carry the whole weight because I thought evidence would matter more when the time was right.”

Ardin smiled without warmth. “And now the time is right because the condemned woman has discovered remorse?”

“No. The time is right because you ordered another flood.”

Ardin reached for the master cutout. The guards raised their weapons.

“If you sever the network,” Tomas said, “the chamber below loses its timing reference. The pressure sequence collapses. You’ll kill everyone still on the assemblies.”

“People already dying?” Ardin asked. “You’ve always been sentimental about numbers after the fact.”

The words struck harder than Tomas expected. He opened the maintenance book and laid it on the console.

“I was there,” he said. “I heard his warning. I saw what Mara did. I know exactly what she caused. That is why your lie cannot stand. Not because she is innocent. Because you made her guilt useful.”

Ardin’s hand hovered above the cutout.

Below them, the city answered. Bells from the lower stations began ringing—not the Council’s pattern, not the old resistance signal, but irregular calls from tower to tower. Guards were opening routes. Survivors were taking controls. Citizens were speaking over public receivers, shouting names into the channels before the signal could be reclaimed.

In the central chamber, Ilya and Vessa reached the west diversion assembly. The control housing was locked with a Council seal. Vessa broke it with the hook of her pole. Inside, three levers waited beneath painted instructions: NORTH RISE, CONTROLLED LOSS, EMERGENCY LOCK.

“Which one?” Vessa demanded.

“None alone,” Oris called. “The split requires all three held between marks.”

Anik arrived through the rising water, dragging the south relay line. “Then we hold them together.”

Ilya looked at Mara. “You heard him.”

Mara nodded. “No one moves until everyone is ready.”

It was a small sentence. It cost her more than the broadcast.

Juno, white-faced, pushed away from the brace. “I can take the emergency lock.”

“You can barely stand,” Ilya said.

“I can stand long enough.”

From above came a deep mechanical boom. The signal chamber lights went out, then returned red. Ardin had tried the cutout. The system had resisted.

Tomas’s voice burst through the nearest speaker, no longer private. “Ardin is attempting to sever the civic coils. All stations, hold your relays. Repeat: hold your relays.”

Ardin lunged for him. The two guards caught the Councilor before he reached the console. He fought with astonishing strength, shouting that the city would tear itself apart without command.

“It already did,” Tomas said, and forced his hand away from the switch.

Below, water surged through the chamber. Mara felt the wheel spin against her grip. Vessa seized the west lever. Anik locked the south. Ilya braced Juno at the emergency housing, while Oris called the timing count.

“Now,” Mara said.

They pulled.

The engine gave a sound like a bell breaking. Pressure divided through the old channels. The water rose, but no single district took the whole force. Somewhere beyond the walls, a gate opened. Then another. The city’s remaining warning towers carried the change outward in uneven, living pulses.

For the first time, Veyr was not listening to one voice.

It was answering.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Mara is at the north manual assembly in the central tidal chamber, waist-deep in rising water, both burned or cut hands gripping the return wheel. Her temple wound, cough, exhaustion, and shame persist. She has broadcast through every surviving channel, naming the dead, admitting she caused devastation by ignoring Tomas’s warning and choosing simultaneous sabotage, and releasing the Council’s records and final-flood plans. She has relinquished control of the public narrative and now insists that every crew agree before a gate is moved. She is committed to the split-pressure plan and saving whoever can be reached without declaring anyone expendable. She carries the canvas instrument case with the Council copies, Tower Three casualty assessment, Ardin’s order, tide compass, pencils, signal wire, and tools. She knows guards are mutinying and the public is hearing conflicting truths.

set.name: Sere Ardin
set.description: Ardin is in the signal chamber above the central tidal chamber, attempting to sever the civic coils and reclaim command after his fabricated confession was exposed. He has been confronted by Tomas and restrained by mutinous guards, but remains defiant and dangerous. His authority is collapsing, his orders to abandon the undercity are being disobeyed, and he still believes only centralized command can prevent Veyr from tearing itself apart.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Tomas is in the signal chamber with two mutinous guards, confronting Ardin at the master cutout. He is wounded or exhausted but functional, carrying copied enclave records, buried-cache evidence, the archival maintenance book, Ardin’s order, and preserved evacuation and alteration records. He has heard Mara’s confession and publicly acknowledged his own role in preserving the Council’s lie. He is preventing Ardin from severing the civic coils and remains committed to keeping the signal open and the split-pressure plan honest rather than controlling its outcome.

set.name: Juno Sarr
set.description: Juno is at the emergency diversion housing in the central tidal chamber, pale and weakened by her high shoulder wound. With Ilya supporting her, she has taken the emergency-lock lever and helped the crews seize the three manual controls. She remains stern and distrustful of vengeance and Council authority, hears that fellow guards are mutinying, and is determined to hold her position long enough to keep the split-pressure sequence alive despite her worsening condition.

set.name: Oris Pell
set.description: Oris is on the central platform under Ilya’s care, pale, coughing, weak from chemical poisoning and painful ribs, and unable to safely walk the assemblies. He continues directing coil load, pressure, and timing. He called the lever sequence that began the split-pressure configuration. His engineering knowledge and tools remain essential while the engine fails and the water rises.

set.name: Ilya Renn
set.description: Ilya is in the central tidal chamber at the west diversion assembly, exhausted and favoring her left side. She is stabilizing Oris and Juno while bracing Juno at the emergency control and helping coordinate the survivor crews. She witnessed Mara’s confession and now enforces Mara’s collective decision rule, remaining distrustful of Mara’s tactical instincts but committed to keeping the wounded and refugees from being treated as interchangeable pieces.

set.name: Vessa
set.description: Vessa is at the west manual diversion assembly in the central tidal chamber with her hooked pole and lamp. She broke the Council seal and is holding the west lever as the split-pressure sequence begins. She remains wary of Mara’s authority, grieving the helpers killed in Ardin’s attack and her brother Lio, and is committed to protecting the market-tower survivors while the water rises.

set.name: Anik
set.description: Anik is at the south manual assembly in the central tidal chamber, having dragged and secured the south relay line and pulled the lever with the other crews. He is grieving Senn’s death, furious at the Council’s abandonment order, and still distrustful of promises to save the upper city. He agreed to the collective plan and continues judging Mara by whether she holds the gates without declaring anyone a necessary loss.

set.name: Sergeant Dain
set.description: Sergeant Dain has turned against Ardin’s abandonment order at an East Rise guard station after hearing Mara’s confession and seeing the final-flood plan. He struck aside his captain’s weapon, opened the south stores, and is leading mutinous guards with rescue boats toward the lower sluices. He is armed, angry, and committed to reaching people in the undercity, though he has not yet reached the central chamber.

Mara’s unedited confession and the released evacuation ledgers, diversion maps, casualty assessment, final-flood plan, and Ardin’s orders reached surviving receivers across the lower districts, North Rise, guard stations, and public channels, forcing Veyr to confront both Council sacrifice and Mara’s responsibility.

Guards at multiple stations refused Ardin’s order to abandon the undercity and secure North Rise; Sergeant Dain struck down his captain’s weapon, opened the south stores, and led a mutiny toward the lower sluices.

Tomas reached the signal chamber with mutinous guards and confronted Ardin, preventing him from severing the civic coils and exposing that the Council had made Mara’s guilt useful to conceal its own planned flood.

Ilya, Vessa, Anik, Juno, and the survivor crews seized the manual diversion controls and pulled the three levers together, beginning the collective split-pressure sequence while the engine and chamber continued to flood.

The mutinous guards and lower-district survivors must hold the opened routes while the failing engine is operated in reduced configuration, allowing as many people as possible to escape before the next surge.

chapters.name: The Reduced Configuration
chapters.content:
## The Reduced Configuration

The first sound was not the bell but the engine’s refusal to turn.

The great drums shuddered beneath the chamber. Their teeth struck once, twice, then slipped with a groan that passed through the water and into Mara’s bones. The rising tide around her waist trembled as if the cavern itself had drawn breath and could not release it.

“Pressure’s climbing on the east side,” Oris called from the platform. His voice came thin through the iron roar. “West return is taking load. South relay is dead.”

Anik swore. “Then give it more.”

“More is what killed it.”

Mara looked across the chamber. Lamps swung from hooks and made broken moons on the water. Vessa held the west lever with both hands, her hooked pole wedged beneath the housing. At the south assembly, Anik had looped the relay line around his chest. Ilya stood between the central platform and Juno, one hand pressed to Oris’s ribs and the other clamped over the captain’s shoulder wound. Juno’s face had gone gray, but she still held the emergency-lock lever upright.

Above them, through the shaft grilles, came a new sound: distant shouting, then the hollow slap of oars. Dain’s mutineers had reached the lower sluices. The opened routes were carrying people out. They were also carrying the flood in.

“How many routes?” Mara asked.

“Three that we can hold,” Ilya answered. “The market tower’s moving. Vessa’s people are bringing the children through the north culvert. Dain has boats at South Reach, but the old streets are breaking behind them.”

“North Rise?”

“Still dry,” Oris said. “For now.”

The question waited in the machinery. Preserve the upper city and let the condemned districts take the surge. Save the greatest number by closing the lower channels. Or force every gate open, attempt a total rescue, and tear the engine apart before anyone could escape.

Mara felt the old desire rise in her with the water: take the levers, choose the sequence, make the city obey one mind. It arrived dressed as arithmetic. It called itself necessity.

“Show me the load,” she said.

Oris coughed, spat pink into the flood, and pointed to the slate Vessa had carried from the platform. Numbers crawled down it in chalk. “The civic coils are failing. We can restart the original balance only if all six assemblies answer. They won’t. The south relay has water in its contacts, and the east shutter is jammed. If I bypass both, the return channel takes the entire surge.”

“North Rise?”

“Flooded in eleven minutes.”

“Lower districts?”

“Flooded in four if we close the return. Market tower in six if we leave the west open.”

Anik’s eyes found hers. “You know what he’s saying.”

“Yes.”

“Say it where everyone can hear.”

The chamber seemed to lean toward her. Mara tightened her hands on the north wheel. The metal was hot beneath the water, and the skin across her palms had split again.

“We cannot save every district,” she said. “The engine will not carry a full configuration. If we force it, the drums shear, the cavern fills, and no route remains open. If we preserve North Rise, the lower districts take the surge. If we preserve the lower routes and the refuge, part of North Rise will flood.”

“Part?” Vessa shouted. “Which part?”

Oris lifted his head. “We can reduce the pressure by taking the western return and feathering the north shutter. It will save the market tower, South Reach boats, and the central rises. It will not save District Four or the old glassworks. The pressure there is already too high.”

A man near Vessa yelled, “Then open everything!”

“No,” Ilya said. She did not shout, but the word carried. “That kills the people already moving.”

“Close the lower gates,” Anik said. “Save the most.”

“Which most?” Mara asked.

He flinched, not from the question but from hearing his own demand placed in the open. Behind him, the south relay line jerked as something struck it underwater.

Mara remembered the shelter gates. The pounding from the other side. Her own hands on a control housing while the city became a diagram. She had believed that if she could only find the right sequence, the deaths would become an accusation clean enough to compel the living.

There was no clean sequence. There were only people inside the numbers, and people who would have to be told what could not be done.

“Everyone speaks for their route,” Mara said. “Not for the city. Not for justice. Your route. What can it carry, and whom can it reach?”

Vessa stared at her, suspicious even now. Then she looked toward the shaft. “West culvert carries the market tower if we keep the gate half-open. Full opening tears the culvert roof down. I have eighty people moving. Maybe a hundred.”

“South,” Anik said. “Dain has six boats. The old pump road reaches the rise, but only if the south relay stays live.”

“North,” Oris said. “North Rise can take the central hospital and the upper wards. But not all of North Rise. The low terraces will go.”

“East,” said a survivor Mara did not know. “Glassworks is already gone.”

The words struck harder than any alarm. Gone, before the gate had moved. A condemned district erased not by a decision in this chamber but by the design waiting inside the engine.

Juno’s knees buckled. Ilya caught her beneath the arm.

“Captain,” Ilya said. “You need to leave the lever.”

Juno’s fingers tightened. “If I leave, the emergency housing slams shut.”

“We can brace it.”

“No.” Juno looked at Mara. “The brace is rotten. You know that.”

Mara did. The emergency housing had a manual catch beneath the lever, a narrow iron tongue that had to be held down while the return wheel engaged. It required a body at the assembly. It had always required a body; the Council’s plans had simply called that body an operator.

“Juno,” Mara said, “we can rotate the sequence and bring you out before the third pressure rise.”

“Can we?”

Oris looked away.

The captain gave a small, humorless smile. “That’s what I thought.”

Ilya shook her head. “No. We find another way.”

“That is another way,” Juno said. “It is the way that keeps the gate from killing everyone behind it.”

Mara wanted to command her to release it. She wanted to promise that the numbers were wrong, that there was one hidden channel, one overlooked maintenance path, one act of will that could make the chamber generous. The promise formed, familiar and lethal.

She swallowed it.

“Juno,” she said, “do you consent to hold the emergency catch?”

The captain’s expression changed. Not softened. Not forgiven. But the question reached her as a person instead of a component.

“I consent,” Juno said. “And I order no one to call it noble.”

“Agreed.”

“Juno—” Ilya began.

“Ilya, you keep Oris breathing. That is your order to yourself. Vessa, move your people. Anik, get that relay live. Mara—”

“I’m listening.”

“Do not make my death balance your old one.”

Mara’s breath broke. She counted the wheel’s spokes: seven, eight, nine. “I won’t.”

They worked.

Ilya secured Oris to the platform with signal wire and wrapped his ribs tight enough that he could direct the coil loads without falling. Vessa sent runners into the west passage, each carrying a lamp hooded against the spray. Anik stripped the south relay with his knife and plunged both hands into the sparking housing. The current snapped blue around his wrists.

Mara turned the north wheel a quarter stroke. The engine screamed. Somewhere below, a gate opened against the pressure and a wall collapsed with a sound like a mountain breaking.

“Now!” Oris cried.

Vessa hauled the west lever down. Anik shouted that the south line had taken. Juno drove the emergency catch beneath the housing and held it there as the lever bucked against her shoulder.

Water surged through the chamber. It struck Mara hard enough to lift her feet. The canvas case tore from its strap and vanished into the black. She caught the strap at the last instant, dragging it against her chest. Council copies, casualty assessment, Ardin’s order—the paper mattered because people had died and the living would lie about why. She would not let the water take the record.

“North shutter!” Oris yelled. “Feather it! Not close—feather!”

Mara turned the wheel by inches. Each adjustment changed the chamber’s voice. A deep bellow became a grinding moan, then a shriek. Through the eastern grilles she saw buildings fold into the flood: the glassworks roof, three terraces, a row of worker houses whose windows flashed with lamps. People were still running on the upper walkways.

“Can we hold them?” Anik shouted.

“No,” Oris answered. “If we divert more, the west culvert collapses.”

A child’s lamp bobbed in the distance. Then it disappeared.

Mara’s hands moved toward the wheel’s full-open position.

Ilya seized her wrist. “No.”

“They’re there.”

“And so are the people behind us.”

“Open it and we save more.”

“Open it and the engine tears. You know that.”

The old argument wore a new face. Not terror this time, but mercy. Not command, but refusal to accept the boundary. Mara looked at the water, at the lamp-lit routes, at Juno shaking beneath the emergency lever.

“I know,” she said.

She turned the wheel back.

The reduced configuration caught.

The central drum began to rotate, slowly at first, its immense teeth meshing with a force that shook dust from the ceiling. The west channel held. In the shaft above, voices multiplied—survivors climbing, guards hauling strangers into boats, someone laughing with the wild disbelief of the spared. The market tower’s route remained open.

Then the emergency housing split.

Juno cried out. The lever slammed sideways, pinning her against the iron frame. Ilya lunged, but Juno kicked the brace loose before she could reach her.

“Keep the sequence!” Juno shouted.

Mara released the north wheel and crossed the flood toward her. The water was chest-deep now. “I can pull you free.”

“Not without dropping the catch.”

“There has to be—”

“Do not.” Juno’s voice cut through the roar. “You asked me. I answered. Let me answer for myself.”

Mara stopped.

Juno’s face was white, her eyes clear. Beyond her, the gates held their unequal tensions: west half-open, south alive, north feathered. The machinery was saving some because they had chosen where it could save them. It was not justice. It was not absolution. It was a limit they had refused to disguise.

“Tell them,” Juno said, breath by breath, “the gate stayed open.”

“I will.”

“And tell them I was afraid.”

Mara’s throat closed. “I will.”

“Good.”

The next pressure rise came. Iron screamed. Juno’s hand slipped from the catch, then found it again. Ilya reached Mara and pulled her backward as the housing buckled inward. For one instant Juno seemed to stand inside a white wall of water, still holding the lever, still refusing the engine’s hunger.

Then the wall closed.

The chamber lurched. The north drum locked, shuddered, and continued turning. The west passage remained open. South lights moved upward through the shaft in a wavering chain.

“Juno!” Ilya screamed.

Mara could not answer. She gripped the north wheel until the spokes cut her palms and watched the water carry splintered wood, a torn guard cloak, and one brass captain’s badge past her knees.

Above, the bells began to ring—not the impossible unified peal she had once made, but separate signals from separate districts. West. South. North. Uneven, damaged, alive.

Oris sagged against the platform. “Configuration stable,” he whispered. “Reduced, but stable.”

Mara looked toward the eastern dark where District Four had vanished. Then toward the shaft where the rescued climbed. The city had not been saved. The city had not been punished. It had been divided by water, by design, by choices made too late and choices made long ago.

“Stable for how long?” she asked.

Oris closed his eyes. “Until the next failure.”

Mara nodded. There would be work after survival. There would be names, testimony, graves, and people who would say the compromise was murder. Some would say it was mercy. Both might be true.

She loosened her grip on the wheel.

“Then we keep it stable,” she said. “And we tell them exactly what it cost.”

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Mara is at the north manual assembly in the central tidal chamber, waist- to chest-deep in rising water, hands split and burned, temple wound and cough persisting. She turned the north wheel to feather the shutter and accepted the collectively chosen reduced split-pressure configuration rather than sacrificing the lower districts, preserving the market-tower route, South Reach boats, and central rises while District Four, the glassworks, and other lower terraces collapsed. She witnessed Juno’s loss while holding the emergency catch. Mara recovered and retains the canvas instrument case containing Council copies, the Tower Three casualty assessment, Ardin’s order, tide compass, pencils, signal wire, and tools. She remains exhausted and ashamed but committed to keeping the temporary configuration stable, accounting for its cost, and telling the truth rather than claiming clean justice or control.

set.name: Juno Sarr
set.description: Juno was at the emergency diversion housing with her high shoulder wound, pale and weakened, when she consented to hold the failing emergency catch so the reduced configuration could engage. The housing collapsed around her during the pressure rise; she is gravely lost or dead beneath the water and wreckage, with her brass captain’s badge carried away. Her last known goal was keeping the gate open, and she instructed Mara to tell the survivors that she was afraid rather than make her sacrifice noble.

set.name: Oris Pell
set.description: Oris is secured to the central platform by signal wire, pale and coughing with chemical poisoning and painful ribs. He directed the coil loads and confirmed that the full engine configuration would fail, then guided the crews into the reduced split-pressure sequence. He reports that the reduced engine is stable only temporarily, until the next failure, and remains essential to monitoring it while survivors evacuate. His tools and engineering knowledge remain with him.

set.name: Ilya Renn
set.description: Ilya is in the central tidal chamber, exhausted and favoring her left side, having stabilized Oris and helped coordinate the survivor crews. She enforced the collective decision rule, stopped Mara from opening the north return fully, and witnessed Juno’s apparent death or loss at the emergency housing. She remains distrustful of Mara’s instincts but committed to keeping the wounded and refugees from being treated as interchangeable pieces; she must continue caring for Oris and help with evacuation and the search for Juno.

set.name: Vessa
set.description: Vessa is at the west manual diversion assembly with her hooked pole and lamp, having held the west lever half-open while runners moved roughly eighty to one hundred market-tower survivors through the culvert. The west route held, though the surrounding lower districts collapsed. She remains wary of Mara, grieving the dead, and committed to moving the refuge and documenting what the reduced configuration saved and cost.

set.name: Anik
set.description: Anik is at the south manual assembly, with the relay line secured around him, having restored the damaged south relay by hand while the reduced configuration engaged. The South Reach boats and route remained open. He is grieving Senn and furious at the Council, still distrustful of promises, and continues judging Mara by whether she admits the districts sacrificed rather than disguising the compromise as justice.

set.name: Sergeant Dain
set.description: Sergeant Dain is leading mutinous guards and rescue boats through the opened lower routes toward South Reach and the surviving rises. His mutiny helped keep evacuation routes open after hearing Mara’s confession and Ardin’s abandonment order. He has not reached the central chamber and does not yet know Juno’s fate; he remains armed, angry, and committed to rescuing as many lower-district survivors as the reduced configuration permits.

The engine could not sustain a full balancing configuration, so the crews chose a reduced split-pressure sequence: the west route remained half-open, the south relay was restored, and the north shutter was feathered, saving the market-tower refuge, South Reach boats, and central rises while condemning District Four, the glassworks, and other lower terraces.

Juno consented to hold the failing emergency catch so the reduced configuration could engage; the housing collapsed around her during the next pressure rise, leaving her gravely lost or dead while the gate remained open.

The reduced configuration stabilized the engine temporarily, and uneven warning signals from the west, south, and north routes announced that many survivors escaped even as several condemned districts collapsed.
The survivors and mutinous guards must complete the evacuation through the surviving west, south, and north routes before the reduced engine suffers its next failure.
The crews must account for Juno Sarr’s fate at the emergency housing and recover her remains or establish that she survived before leaving the central chamber.
Mara must preserve and deliver the recovered Council records while the survivors document which districts were lost and what the reduced configuration saved.

chapters.name: No Forgiveness Yet
chapters.content:
The water went down by degrees, as if the city were reluctant to reveal what it had done.

At first it withdrew from the central chamber only far enough to uncover the tops of the rails. Then the stone steps emerged, black with silt and shining under the lamps. Bodies came into view in the hollows between the machinery: two of Ardin’s agents, three survivors who had been working the west assembly, a guard whose name no one knew. The engine ticked and groaned around them, holding its reduced configuration like a wounded animal holding its breath.

“Don’t call it stable,” Oris said whenever anyone used the word. He sat on the central platform with his ribs bound in strips of sailcloth, one hand clamped over his poisoned chest. “Call it not yet failing.”

Not yet failing became the measure of the day.

Runners went through the west culvert with lamps hooded against the dark. They returned carrying names, numbers, and conflicting accounts. The market tower had emptied most of its upper floors. South Reach boats had taken on families from the flooded terraces, though two had overturned against the broken quay. The central rises were crowded beyond capacity. District Four was gone below the second level. The glassworks had collapsed into its own canals, carrying fire and powdered silica across the water.

Vessa made the runners repeat each account until she could mark it on the damp map. Anik stood beside her, jaw clenched, recording the dead in a ledger taken from the engine office. Every few minutes he looked toward Mara.

“Write the names,” he said. “Not ‘losses.’ Not ‘unavoidable casualties.’ Names.”

“I am writing them,” Mara said.

“Then write the districts that were chosen.”

Her pencil paused. “Chosen by whom?”

“By all of us.”

The answer struck harder than accusation. Anik bent over the ledger again. Mara looked at the map: west half-open, south restored, north narrowed until the pressure would not break the upper rises. A line of blue pencil crossed the lower terraces, the places the reduced configuration had surrendered. She had drawn that line herself.

They found Juno at the emergency housing when the water fell below the iron braces. The catch had held. The housing had not.

Her body lay beneath a slab of fractured stone, one shoulder still pressed against the manual bar. The brass captain’s badge was gone, but the red cord from her uniform had caught on a tooth of the mechanism. Ilya knelt in the mud and closed Juno’s eyes. No one spoke the word sacrifice. Mara remembered Juno’s last instruction and said, “She was afraid.”

Ilya’s hands tightened around the edge of the stone. “Yes.”

“She asked us to tell them.”

“Then tell them all of it.”

So they did. They lifted Juno out with a rope line and carried her to the upper platform, where Vessa wrapped her in a sailcloth marked with the names of the first dead. There was no ceremony. There was too much work, and no one trusted a ceremony that might turn a frightened woman into a clean symbol.

By the time Sergeant Dain reached the chamber, the Council had ceased to exist in every way that mattered except on paper.

He came in a stolen patrol skiff with six guards and seventeen survivors packed into it. His coat was torn, his face streaked with soot, and he carried three weapons belonging to men who had refused his mutiny. Behind him, the guards unloaded sacks of bread, medical cloth, and seized Council seals.

“Ardin’s secured,” Dain said. “Tomas took him alive in the signal chamber. He tried to reach the master cutout. We bound him to the rail and brought him up under watch.”

“Alive,” Anik said. “Why?”

Dain looked at Mara. “Because we’re done letting frightened men decide that killing is administration.”

No one cheered. The survivors had no strength for it. A woman from the market tower spat into the water and asked whether that meant Mara would be allowed to live as well.

The question traveled through the chamber faster than any order.

Some wanted Mara hanged from the old warning tower. Some wanted her returned to the Bastion, where a sentence already existed and required no argument. Others, especially the mechanics and pump workers, insisted she was the only person who could keep the reduced engine from failing before the evacuation ended. One boy with a bandaged cheek shouted that the Bellmaker should repair every bell she had broken. An older man answered that no one should put a knife back into the hand that had cut them, even if the knife was needed to cut rope.

Mara listened from beside the north assembly, unable to keep her eyes from the place where Juno had lain.

“You’re enjoying this,” Ilya said.

Mara turned. “What?”

“Being necessary. Being hated. Having every choice point toward you.”

The old reflex rose in Mara—deny, counter, identify the weakness in the accusation. She counted the rivets in the nearest housing instead. Seven visible. Two rusted. One missing.

“I don’t know how to enjoy it,” she said.

“That isn’t the same as not wanting it.”

“No.” Mara looked toward Oris, who was arguing with three workers about the next pressure cycle. “It isn’t.”

The argument over her fate followed them out of the chamber and into the city.

Veyr had survived, but survival did not restore order. The Council hall was occupied by clerks, guards, widows, pump workers, and two rival committees that each claimed to be the provisional authority. Notices appeared on walls and were torn down within the hour. One promised tribunals. Another promised immediate executions. A third called for the restoration of the old civic hierarchy until “proper calm” returned.

Mara was taken to the former customs house under guard—not imprisoned, the guards insisted, though they locked the door from the outside. The room smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and the river. Her canvas case rested on the table before her. She checked its contents by touch: copied Council orders, Tower Three’s casualty assessment, Ardin’s final-flood directive, tide compass, pencils, signal wire, tools. All present.

The records were safer in her possession than in any archive, but possession felt too much like control. She pushed the case away.

Tomas arrived after sunset with two clerks and a bandage around his forearm. He looked older than he had that morning. Perhaps the city had removed the last reason to pretend otherwise.

“Ardin is being held in the signal chamber,” he said. “The remaining Councilors are under guard. Three attempted to flee through the north gates. The records we released have been copied in six districts.”

“And the people who copied them?”

“Some are calling for your execution. Some are calling for mine.”

“Good.”

His expression tightened. “I gave evidence today.”

“Against Ardin?”

“Against all of them. The seawall schedules. The labor-compound orders. The altered maintenance books. My own signatures.” He placed a packet on the table. “I included the parts that implicate me.”

Mara did not open it. “You have been including those parts for twelve years?”

“No.”

The answer was clean. It left no place to hide.

Tomas sat across from her. “I told the tribunal’s commissioners that I signed the prepared account. That I accepted the investigator’s post. That I withheld the maintenance warning because I was afraid, and because I thought I could preserve the evidence until the right moment. I told them that waiting protected me more reliably than it protected the truth.”

“Did they applaud?”

“One of them cried.”

“Then you have already been forgiven.”

“No.” He looked at the wet window. “They were only surprised that a man in uniform could be guilty.”

For a moment, Mara saw the old Tomas: sleeves rolled, fingers blackened with grease, leaning over a current map while rain struck the Signal Office windows. Then the image altered. His hand was signing her name into a public lie. His mouth was saying deliberate sabotage, not massacre. The distinction had mattered to him. It had not saved anyone.

“They will use my testimony,” he said. “They need a proceeding that looks like judgment.”

“They need a new monster.”

“They need more than one kind of truth.”

Mara almost laughed. “That is what we said before.”

“Yes.” Tomas met her gaze. “This time we have to remain when it becomes inconvenient.”

The provisional tribunal came the next morning. It consisted of a market-tower elder, a South Reach boatmaster, a former Council clerk, a physician from the elevated hospital, and a judge who had removed her civic chain before entering. None wore the same insignia. That was meant to reassure Mara. It did not.

The boatmaster spoke first. “The engine will fail again. Oris says the temporary balance may last days, perhaps less. You know the old warning network. You can help rebuild it.”

“I can.”

“You can help design a system with no district hidden from the others,” said the clerk. “Every signal copied everywhere. Public maintenance books. Rotating authority. Your knowledge would be difficult to replace.”

“And my sentence?”

The physician folded her hands. “Freedom. A public position in reconstruction. Immunity for the original flood and for actions taken during the emergency, provided you testify fully and work under the tribunal’s supervision.”

The offer was the shape of a door. Mara could feel the cold air beyond it.

“You want the Bellmaker to build the bells,” she said.

“We want Mara Venn,” said the elder, “if she is willing to be more than what they called her.”

“I am willing to be what I did.”

The judge’s face hardened. “The Council engineered two floods. It concealed the evacuation plan, sacrificed whole districts, and made you carry the public blame. Refusing immunity may satisfy grief, but it will not repair a gate.”

“No,” Mara said. “It will not.”

She opened the canvas case and laid the documents on the table. Her fingers were still burned, and the paper caught briefly against a split nail.

“Exposing the Council does not return the people at the south shelter. It does not uncollapse the tower. It does not make the chemical water harmless. I connected the charge after Tomas warned me. I wanted the city frightened enough to obey me. I wanted the catastrophe in my hands. I did not intend those deaths, but intention is not the whole measure of a hand.”

The boatmaster studied her. “Then what are you asking?”

“For no bargain.”

“You would choose prison?”

“I would choose a hearing where the evidence against me is not traded for my usefulness.”

“And if the tribunal condemns you?”

“Then the warning network will have to be rebuilt by someone else.”

Outside, a bell rang from the market tower. One short note, then silence. A runner shouted that the west gauge had shifted. People moved in the street, carrying ropes and ledgers and bodies. The city had not become just because the Council had fallen. It had only become responsible for what came next.

Tomas gathered the evidence into a neat stack. “You understand they may imprison you for life.”

“Yes.”

“They may execute you.”

Mara looked at the dead written on Anik’s ledger, at Juno’s red cord lying beside the lamp, at the case that held the proof of crimes both hers and the Council’s.

“Yes.”

The judge rose. “You refuse immunity.”

“I refuse the idea that truth is payment.”

No one answered. There was no forgiveness in the room, and no clean vengeance either. Only the records, the names, the unstable engine, and the work of carrying what could still be carried.

When the tribunal left, Mara remained at the table beneath the locked door. She took up her pencil and began copying the casualty list into a second ledger. Not losses. Not collateral. Names.

At the bottom of the first page she wrote Juno Sarr, captain, afraid, held the gate.

Then she turned the page and continued.

chapters.name: The Open Gate
chapters.content:
The Open Gate

The first morning after the Council fell, Mara was given a room with a door that opened outward.

She noticed before she noticed the light.

In the Mirror Bastion, every door opened inward, toward the prisoner, so that the wardens could stand beyond the hinge and make the geometry of release their own. Twelve years of waking had taught Mara to measure the angle of each opening, the scrape of the latch, the interval between key and footstep. This door had no mirror-glass in it. Its hinges were on the corridor side. Someone had removed the lock plate and replaced it with a guard seated on a stool.

The guard was young enough to have been born after the Night of Bells.

“Up,” he said.

Mara was already up. She sat at the table in the former customs house, her burned hands resting beside the ledger. The room smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and the medicinal bitter of Ilya’s salve. Her cough had settled into her ribs like a tenant who intended to stay. Through the warped window she could see the lower roofs shining under a gray dawn. Smoke rose from the glassworks district, though there was little glass left to burn.

On the table lay two columns of names.

The left was the list recovered from the old casualty assessment: tower collapse, chemical release, sealed shelter, flood surge. The right was Vessa’s and Anik’s newer account, written in different hands and corrected by people who had survived the places the Council had reduced to figures. A name was not a unit. A name had a mother, a trade, a quarrel unfinished, a favorite cup, a debt, a child waiting at a landing that no longer existed.

Mara had copied until the pencil blistered her palm.

“Tribunal clerks are asking for you,” the guard said.

“Which clerks?”

He hesitated. “The ones who are not Council clerks.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one I have.”

She looked at him. The old Mara would have tested his route, his fear, his likely response to a false alarm. She would have found the weak point in the sentence and pressed it until the door, the guard, and the morning belonged to her.

Instead she closed the ledger.

“Take me to the signal yard first.”

The guard glanced toward the corridor. Two others waited there, weapons lowered but visible. “I was told to take you to the hearing room.”

“Then you were told badly. The first bell is being lifted.”

A woman’s voice came from the doorway. “Let her see it.”

Ilya stood behind the guards with her left arm bound close to her body. Her face was gray from exhaustion, and one strand of hair had escaped the knot at her nape. She carried no medical bag. That absence made Mara understand how far the city had fallen: even Ilya had run out of things to mend.

“The tribunal agreed,” Ilya said. “Under guard. No private access to the coils. No commands.”

Mara nodded. “Good.”

Ilya studied her. “You say that as if the restrictions are comforting.”

“They are clear.”

“Clear is not the same as fair.”

“No.” Mara looked toward the open door. “But it is more than I was owed yesterday.”

They crossed the customs house yard where survivors had hung blankets from the broken cranes. The blankets made a new architecture, temporary walls dividing cooking fires from sleeping spaces, children from the dead, the living from the water that still climbed in the gutters when the engine shuddered. Sergeant Dain stood at the gate with three mutinous guards. He had lost his helmet and acquired a strip of white cloth around his wrist.

“Signal yard is clear,” he said. “Mostly.”

“Mostly?” Mara asked.

“People keep arriving to tell us what they want the bells to say.”

“Bells do not say what people want.”

Dain gave her a hard look. “That has not stopped anyone.”

The yard had once housed the civic relay tower. Its upper platform had survived, though the tower leaned against the customs house like a drunk seeking shelter. Signal wire ran across the beams in tangled loops. Oris sat on a crate beneath it, ribs bound, his face pinched and yellow from the poison. He held a wrench in one hand and a slate in the other.

“The west coil is holding,” he said. “The south relay is not. If the engine drops pressure again, we lose the lower warning route entirely.”

“Then we repair the south relay before the next cycle.”

“Everyone says that.”

“Everyone is correct.”

Oris snorted. “There she is.”

Mara climbed the scaffold. Each rung struck a bright line of pain through her burned hands. Below, Ilya told the guards to keep clear of the work area. Dain argued with a survivor carrying a basket of copper scraps. The woman won the argument and placed the basket beside Oris’s crate.

At the top, Mara found the old bell housing split along its seam. Inside, the striker was bent, the contact teeth fused black. She touched the metal with the tip of her finger and remembered another tower, another morning, Tomas saying wait. The memory came without water or screaming. It came as a sentence she had refused to carry.

This will shear.

“Yes,” she said aloud.

Oris looked up. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“No. Not nothing.”

Mara drew the instrument case from the guard who had followed her. The case contained the tide compass, pencils, spare wire, and tools darkened by the central chamber. It also contained copies of Ardin’s order and the casualty assessment. She took out the wire.

“Who approved the replacement?” she asked.

“No one,” Oris said. “The districts sent what they had.”

“Then we mark the splice.”

“With whose seal?” Dain called.

“No seal.” She looked down at him. “Mark it with the names of the districts that supplied it.”

The basket woman laughed once, without humor. “So when it fails, we know whom to blame?”

“So when it holds, we know whom to thank.”

“No,” the woman said. “When it fails, we know where to go.”

Mara considered this. “That too.”

They worked through the morning. Not as she had once worked, with instructions issued from the center and bodies arranged around them, but in a constant exchange of hands and objections. Oris gave the sequence; Mara checked the tolerances. A dockworker held the bracket while a girl from South Reach threaded the wire. Dain sent guards to fetch insulation from the upper stores and returned with half the needed amount because the rest had been claimed by a shelter on Ninth Rise. Mara altered the configuration rather than ordering it taken.

At midday, the young guard brought her water.

“What is your name?” Mara asked.

“Lio.”

“District?”

“North Rise.”

She waited. He seemed embarrassed by the answer.

“Say it plainly,” she said.

“North Rise.”

“Were you there when the broadcast came through?”

“My mother was. We heard your voice.”

Mara’s hand tightened around the cup. “Which voice?”

“The real one, I think.”

“There was no real one. There was the voice I used.”

Lio looked at the wires. “You said your name.”

“I did.”

“You said you killed people.”

“I did.”

“And that the Council killed people.”

“Yes.”

He was silent for several breaths. Mara counted them despite herself: four, five, six. The old regimen rose like a wall. She let it fall.

“Are you a hero?” he asked. “Or a monster?”

The yard seemed to grow quiet, though the hammering continued. Somewhere below, someone was crying over a list. Beyond the roofs, the water shifted in the streets with a soft, patient sound.

Mara looked at the boy. He had a cut across his cheek and copper dust on his sleeve. He had probably carried wire from a district whose name would appear in Vessa’s ledger before evening. He wanted a shape that could hold what had happened. Hero. Monster. The words were doors, and every door in Veyr had once been built to keep someone outside.

“I am not either,” she said.

Lio frowned. “Then what are you?”

“Responsible.”

“For everything?”

“No.” The answer cost more than the first. “For what I did. For the warning I ignored. For choosing the spectacle. For the people who died because my choices made their deaths possible. The Council is responsible for what it did. Those truths do not cancel each other.”

“Will they punish you?”

“I do not know.”

“Do you want them to?”

Mara looked at the open gate of the yard, the guards beyond it, the people moving freely through the ruin. “I want them to judge me without needing me to be useful.”

Lio seemed dissatisfied. “That is not the same.”

“No,” Mara said. “It is not.”

By late afternoon, the bell housing was ready. Oris descended slowly from the scaffold, refusing Ilya’s offered arm until his knees gave way. Mara secured the last contact herself. The striker had been made from a length of rail salvaged from the submerged tram line—the route she had once forced the expedition to take. On its side, someone had scratched three words: SOUTH REACH, MARKET TOWER, DISTRICT FOUR.

“Those are not all the districts,” Mara said.

“They are the ones who brought metal,” Oris replied.

“Then add the rest when they do.”

The signal yard filled before sunset. Survivors came from the market refuge, the south boats, the central rises, and the temporary camps along the old customs road. Vessa arrived with her ledger under one arm and Anik with a relay box held against his chest. Ilya stood beside them. Dain posted guards, then removed two barricades when the crowd objected that the bell belonged to them.

Mara remained on the platform under watch.

No one asked her to speak. That was the first mercy of the day.

Oris raised his hand. The relay line clicked. Once. Twice. The bell shuddered in its housing, and for an instant Mara expected the metal to split, the tower to fold, the city to answer with water.

Then it rang.

The sound was smaller than the bells of her memory. It did not roll like a command over all Veyr. It traveled in a rough, bright pulse through the repaired wire, down toward the south, across the market tower, up to North Rise. Other bells answered—late, uneven, human. One from the refuge. One from a rooftop near the glassworks. One so faint it might have been struck by a hand rather than a mechanism.

No district was silent by design.

Mara listened until the echoes thinned. The sound did not belong to her. It did not belong to the Council, or to the tribunal, or to the story that had made her into the Bellmaker. It belonged to the people who had carried the wire, argued over the splice, marked the rail, and refused to let a warning become an order.

Tomas found her after dark outside the hearing chamber.

His bandaged forearm was held against his chest. He looked as if sleep had become another accusation.

“They will call the first session at dawn,” he said.

“Will you testify?”

“Yes.”

“Truthfully?”

He met her eyes. “As far as I can.”

“That is not enough.”

“No.” He swallowed. “It is what I have.”

The chamber doors stood open. Inside, clerks arranged papers beneath lamps. Through the inner windows Mara could see no judge’s chair yet, only an empty table and three bowls of fresh water. The tribunal had not decided what shape its authority would take. Perhaps no one in Veyr knew how to build a judgment after the city had learned that its official walls were made of lies.

Tomas remained beside her. “I am sorry,” he said.

Mara watched the lamps tremble in the draft. “I know.”

“Do you forgive me?”

“No.”

He closed his eyes, and she saw him accept the answer rather than attempt to alter it.

“Will you ever?”

“I do not know.”

That, too, was more than she had once allowed herself to say.

A clerk called her name from within.

Mara entered the threshold, then stopped. Behind her, the outer gate of the customs yard remained open. Beyond it waited the repaired bell, the survivors, the guards who had disobeyed, the ledgers, the drowned districts, and all the people whose memories would not be made orderly for her comfort.

She had spent twelve years believing control was the last defense against terror. Now she understood that surrendering control did not make terror vanish. It only stopped her from mistaking possession for repair.

The clerk called again.

Mara placed both burned hands on the doorframe. She did not ask who would believe her. She did not ask whether the sentence would be death, confinement, labor, or something no one had yet named. She did not ask for forgiveness.

She stepped inside to await judgment.

Behind her, the gate stayed open, and the bell began again—one signal for every district, carried by no single voice.
